title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
順天府鄉試錄序
隆慶庚午秋八月順天當鄉
試府臣以考試官請
上命右諭德臣士羙修撰臣時行
往典厥事臣士羙方供事
講幄自惟章句賤流無裨
聖學誠蚤夜祗惕廼茲復叨
===
任使又惟先是丁卯嘗濫竽斯
役今再承
寵命深懼闇劣無能甄拔愈惴惴
不自勝因是心自盟曰所不
惟至公至慎顓精翕慮以圖
報塞者非夫也廼以七日壬
寅

punctuated:
順天府鄉試錄序

隆慶庚午秋八月，順天當鄉試，府臣以考試官請。上命右諭德臣士羙、修撰臣時行往典厥事。臣士羙方供事講幄，自惟章句賤流，無裨聖學，誠蚤夜祗惕。廼茲復叨任使，又惟先是丁卯嘗濫竽斯役，今再承寵命，深懼闇劣，無能甄拔，愈惴惴不自勝。因是心自盟曰：「所不惟至公至慎，顓精翕慮，以圖報塞者，非夫也。」廼以七日壬寅，
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the autumn, in the eighth month of the gengwu year of Longqing [1570], Shuntian was due to hold its Provincial Examination. The prefectural officials requested the appointment of Examiners. His Majesty commanded your servants Shimei, Right Mentor, and Shixing, Senior Compiler, to go and preside over the examination. I, your servant Shimei, was then serving at the imperial lectures. Reflecting that I was merely a lowly scholar occupied with textual explication, unable to contribute to the sage learning of His Majesty, I was truly reverent and apprehensive morning and night. Now I had again been favored with an assignment. I further recalled that in the preceding dingmao year [1567] I had already occupied this post without deserving it. Receiving this gracious command a second time, I deeply feared that my ignorance and inadequacy would leave me unable to discern and select worthy candidates. My anxiety grew beyond my power to contain it. I therefore pledged to myself: “If I do not exercise the utmost impartiality and care, concentrating my energies and gathering my thoughts to endeavor to repay this favor, I am no man.” Then, on the seventh day, renyin, …

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
陞辭入院偕同事諸臣首以所
自盟心者道語之胥戒胥飭
而後從事於是進提學御史
臣李輔所選士暨諸曹六館
所選士凡四千一百有竒三
試之遵
宸斷增額取中式者一百五十人
===
又以所拔優者文二十篇稍
加刪潤為錄
獻焉欽
成命也臣士美拜手稽首序諸簡
端臣聞古昔帝王之興道致
治也未始不以得賢為急務
其取賢斂才也亦未始不以

陞辭入院，偕同事諸臣，首以所自盟心者道語之，胥戒胥飭，而後從事。於是進提學御史臣李輔所選士，暨諸曹六館所選士，凡四千一百有竒，三試之。遵宸斷增額，取中式者一百五十人。又以所拔優者文二十篇，稍加刪潤，為錄獻焉，欽成命也。
臣士美拜手稽首，序諸簡端。臣聞古昔帝王之興道致治也，未始不以得賢為急務；其取賢斂才也，亦未始不以
translation_en:
…I took leave at court and entered the examination compound. Together with my fellow officials, I first conveyed to them the pledge I had made in my heart. We admonished and exhorted one another before undertaking our duties. We then admitted the candidates selected by your servant Li Fu, Censor for the Supervision of Education, together with those selected by the various government offices and the Six Halls of the Imperial University, more than four thousand one hundred in all, and examined them in three sessions. In accordance with Your Majesty’s decision to increase the quota, we selected one hundred and fifty successful candidates. We also took twenty outstanding essays from among those selected, made minor abridgments and refinements, and compiled them into a record for presentation to Your Majesty, reverently fulfilling the imperial command.
Your servant Shimei bows with clasped hands and touches his forehead to the ground, placing this preface at the beginning of the volume. title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
敷求爲先□□子之稱才難
有曰唐虞之際于周爲盛夫
五臣之熙載九人之造周後
世誠莫比其隆矣然在堯舜
則明揚側陋詢岳咨牧嘉言
罔伏野無遺賢在文武則克
知三宅灼見三俊譽髦作人
===
修廢舉逸所以旁求者恒矻
矻也得人之盛良有自哉洪
惟我
國家養士於學校羅才於科目
道本唐虞法鑒周室每三歲
大比士鄉各舉之以爲常
聖

punctuated:
敷求爲先。□□子之稱「才難」，有曰：「唐虞之際，于周爲盛。」夫五臣之熙載、九人之造周，後世誠莫比其隆矣。然在堯舜，則明揚側陋，詢岳咨牧，嘉言罔伏，野無遺賢；在文武，則克知三宅，灼見三俊，譽髦作人，修廢舉逸。所以旁求者恒矻矻也。得人之盛，良有自哉！
洪惟我國家養士於學校，羅才於科目，道本唐虞，法鑒周室。每三歲大比士，鄉各舉之，以爲常。聖
translation_en:
…giving priority to searching far and wide. □□[?] When the Master spoke of the difficulty of finding talented men, he said: “In the age of Tang and Yu and in the Zhou, talent was most abundant.” The five ministers’ splendid accomplishments and the nine men’s establishment of Zhou were indeed achievements whose greatness later ages could not match. Yet under Yao and Shun, men of humble and obscure station were brought to light and promoted; the Four Mountain Chiefs and regional governors were consulted; worthy counsel went unheard nowhere, and no worthy man was left undiscovered in the countryside. Under Kings Wen and Wu, those suited to the three classes of office were duly recognized, and the three classes of outstanding men clearly discerned. Eminent talent was praised and men were cultivated; those who had fallen from office were restored, and those living in retirement were brought forward. Thus their broad search for talent was pursued with unremitting diligence. Such abundance in obtaining worthy men surely had its source!
We reverently reflect that our dynasty nurtures scholars in its schools and gathers talent through the examinations. Its Way is rooted in Tang and Yu, and its institutions take the house of Zhou as their model. Every three years, scholars undergo the great examination, and each locality recommends its men as a regular practice. Sage…

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
聖相承率由兹典□□年来耆卿
碩輔胥此途出後先相望比
於虞周固已無遜也仰惟
皇上以
神聖之資撫
明昌之運
厲精化理
寤寐才賢
踐阼以来
廣進士之額矣
增吉士之選矣間因言者請
詔許天下郡縣學校拔廩生優
異者各一人升于
國學今濟濟賢關皆若人也邇

碩輔胥此途出後先相望比
於虞周固已無遜也仰惟
皇上以
神聖之資撫
明昌之運
厲精化理

增吉士之選矣間因言者請
詔許天下郡縣學校拔廩生優

punctuated: 聖相承，率由兹典。□□年来，耆卿碩輔胥此途出，後先相望，比於虞周，固已無遜也。仰惟皇上以神聖之資，撫明昌之運，厲精化理，寤寐才賢。踐阼以来，廣進士之額矣，增吉士之選矣。間因言者請，詔許天下郡縣學校拔廩生優異者各一人，升于國學。今濟濟賢關，皆若人也。邇
translation_en:
…sage sovereigns have succeeded one another, all following this established practice. Over the past □□ years [?], venerable ministers and eminent chief councillors have all emerged through this path, following one another in succession. Compared with the ages of Yu and Zhou, this certainly falls short in no respect.
We reverently consider how His Majesty, endowed with divine sagacity and presiding over an age of brilliant prosperity, devotes his energies to moral transformation and good government, thinking of talented and worthy men waking and sleeping alike. Since ascending the throne, he has enlarged the quota of metropolitan graduates (jinshi) and increased the number selected as Hanlin bachelors. On one occasion, responding to a proposal submitted to the throne, he issued an edict permitting each prefectural and county school throughout the empire to select one outstanding stipendiary student for promotion to the Directorate of Education. Today, the many worthy men gathered within its gates are all men of this kind. Recently…

translation_en:
…again specially approved the proposal of his scholarly ministers and decreed that the examination quotas of the two capitals each be increased by one tenth. This is an extraordinary act of grace, seldom encountered in the world. How does our Emperor’s eagerness to welcome worthy men differ from that of Yao, Shun, King Wen, and King Wu? Moreover, the capital is the center toward which the four quarters look, the foremost seat of moral excellence, and the first to receive the transforming influence of imperial rule. The many illustrious scholars who hasten to the palace gates, wishing to present their compositions and arguments, are as numerous as rising clouds and gathering mist. Surely among them there must be men of extraordinary distinction who will rise to meet the age and magnify the glorious achievements of the sagely Son of Heaven’s restoration.

Your servant, called upon a second time to fill this post for want of a more capable man, has surveyed the compositions of the many scholars. For the most part, they can elucidate the subtle meanings of the Six Classics, gather together the essential purport of the hundred schools, and analyze…

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
羣言之似敷□□當世之宜廼
與同事者品隲之曰某卷其
言藹如所謂仁義之人也某
卷辭旨豐美所謂得中和之
氣者也某卷文詞温雅所謂
別見孝弟之性者也已而沾
沾喜曰藹藹兹多士乎誠元
===
凱宅俊之流亞也比于往昔
所謂月異而歲不同矣自是
維
君子使庶幾媚于
天子哉時同事者曰吾儕所校者
藝耳未觀其行焉能信之即
若所云得無論篤是與乎臣

translation_en:
…the apparent truths in the various teachings, and expound [two illegible characters] what is appropriate to the present age. I then assessed the papers together with my colleagues, saying: “In this paper, the words convey kindness: its author is what we call a man of benevolence and righteousness. In this paper, the language and meaning are rich and fine: its author is what we call one endowed with the spirit of equilibrium and harmony. In this paper, the diction is gentle and refined: its author is what we call one whose disposition toward filial piety and fraternal respect is especially evident.”
Presently, delighted, I said: “How numerous are these worthy scholars! Truly they rank with the Yuan and Kai, and the eminent men appointed to office [?]. Compared with former times, this is what is meant by ‘different from month to month, and changed from year to year.’ Henceforth, employed by the ruler, may they win the favor of the Son of Heaven!”
At this, my colleagues said: “What we have evaluated is merely their literary skill. We have not observed their conduct; how can we be confident of their character? Even if things are as you say, might this not amount to approving men merely because their discourse is earnest?” Your servant…

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
應之曰不然夫虞廷官人其
惟敷奏周室興賢厥有言揚
因言以知人也久矣而奚疑
耶昔宋儒朱熹嘗推易以觀
天下之人曰凡陽必剛剛必
明明則易知凡陰必柔柔必
暗暗則難測故光明正大疏
===
===
暢洞達無纖芥可疑者必君
子也其依阿淟涊回互隱伏
閃倏狡獪不可方物者必小
人也臣謂文辭之發也亦然
取以校士又安能廋哉然臣
於今兹猶有所厚望焉夫多
士皆

子也其依阿淟涊回互隱伏

士皆
punctuated: 應之曰：「不然。夫虞廷官人，其惟敷奏；周室興賢，厥有言揚。因言以知人也久矣，而奚疑耶？昔宋儒朱熹嘗推《易》以觀天下之人，曰：『凡陽必剛，剛必明，明則易知；凡陰必柔，柔必暗，暗則難測。故光明正大、疏暢洞達、無纖芥可疑者，必君子也；其依阿淟涊、回互隱伏、閃倏狡獪、不可方物者，必小人也。』臣謂文辭之發也亦然，取以校士，又安能廋哉？然臣於今兹猶有所厚望焉。夫多士皆
translation_en: …replied: “Not so. When the court of Shun appointed men to office, it relied on their presentations and reports; when the house of Zhou promoted the worthy, it advanced them on the strength of their words. Knowing people through their words has long been practiced: why doubt it? Zhu Xi, the Confucian scholar of the Song, once extended the principles of the Book of Changes to assess the people of the world, saying: ‘Whatever is yang must be firm; firmness must bring clarity, and clarity makes it easy to know. Whatever is yin must be yielding; yielding must bring obscurity, and obscurity makes it hard to fathom. Thus those who are open, upright, expansive, and penetrating, with not the slightest ground for suspicion, must be gentlemen. Those who are obsequious and sullied, evasive and secretive, elusive and crafty, impossible to classify or fathom, must be petty men.’ Your servant believes that the expression of thoughts in literary compositions follows the same principle. If we use this to assess candidates, how could they conceal themselves? Yet your servant still has great hopes on this occasion. For all these many scholars…

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
先皇豐芑之詒也際
主上敷求之會行將漸鴻振鷺于
帝庭矣其感恩思報以求無負
明時也宜何如用情耶必將有
趾美皐夔追踪旦奭者焉寧
俾元凱宅俊專美有前哉此
臣愚以人事君之意亦
===
皇上增額之至意也多士勗諸是
役也同考則進士臣希夔臣
拱宸臣致中臣汝滙學正臣
邦寵教諭臣邦基臣邦竒臣
一岳臣一位臣起鳳臣浚提
調則府尹臣永祿府丞臣繡
監試則御史臣丕揚臣宗載

監試則御史臣丕揚臣宗載
punctuated:
先皇豐芑之詒也。際主上敷求之會，行將漸鴻振鷺于帝庭矣。其感恩思報，以求無負明時也，宜何如用情耶？必將有趾美皐夔、追踪旦奭者焉，寧俾元凱宅俊專美有前哉？此臣愚以人事君之意，亦皇上增額之至意也。多士勗諸！
是役也，同考則進士臣希夔、臣拱宸、臣致中、臣汝滙，學正臣邦寵，教諭臣邦基、臣邦竒、臣一岳、臣一位、臣起鳳、臣浚；提調則府尹臣永祿、府丞臣繡；監試則御史臣丕揚、臣宗載。
translation_en:
…are the legacy of the late emperor’s nurturing of talent. Now, as His Majesty searches far and wide for worthy men, they will soon advance like wild geese and rise like egrets at the imperial court. How earnestly should they feel gratitude and seek to repay it, striving not to disappoint this enlightened age! Surely among them will be men who carry forward the excellence of Gao and Kui and follow in the footsteps of Dan and Shi. How could they allow the appointment of the Eight Yuan, the Eight Kai, and other outstanding worthies in antiquity alone to enjoy such renown? This is my humble intention in serving my sovereign by providing him with worthy men; it is also His Majesty’s deepest intention in increasing the examination quota. Let all you scholars exert yourselves!
For this examination, the Associate Examiners were your servants Xikui, Gongchen, Zhizhong, and Ruhui, all metropolitan graduates (jinshi); your servant Bangchong, a School Instructor; and your servants Bangji, Bangqi, Yiyue, Yiwei, Qifeng, and Jun, all County School Instructors. The Proctors were your servant Yonglu, Prefect, and your servant Xiu, Prefectural Adjutant. The examination invigilators were your servants Piyang and Zongzai, both Censors.

Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination, fourth year of Longqing (1570).

Proctors

Li Yonglu, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Prefect of Shuntian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Shixue; he was from Changzhi County, Shanxi, and became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the jiachen year.

Song Xun, Grand Master for Central Compliance and Vice Prefect of Shuntian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Bojing; he was from Shangqiu County, Henan, and became a metropolitan graduate in the jiwei year.

Examiners

Ding Shimei, Grand Master for Promoting Instruction, Right Admonisher in the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently Reader-in-waiting in the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Bangyan; he was from Qinghe County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the jiwei year.

Shen Shixing, Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman of the Confucian Community. His courtesy name was Rumo; his registration was in Wu County, Zhili, and he was a native of Changzhou County. He became a metropolitan graduate in the renxu year.

Associate Examiners

Huo Xikui, a metropolitan graduate assigned to duties in the Ministry of Personnel. His courtesy name was Yuqing; his registration was in Yingzhou, Shanxi, and he was a native of Linfen County. He became a metropolitan graduate in the wuchen year.

Qian Gongchen, a metropolitan graduate assigned to duties in the Ministry of Personnel. His courtesy name was Gongqing; he was from Wucheng County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the wuchen year.

Liu Zhizhong, a metropolitan graduate assigned to duties in the Ministry of Personnel. His courtesy name was Weifu; he was from Yanjin County, Henan, and became a metropolitan graduate in the wuchen year.

Sun Ruhui, a metropolitan graduate assigned to duties in the Ministry of Personnel. His courtesy name was Zhonghuan; he was from Yuyao County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the wuchen year.

Duan Bangchong, School Director of the Confucian School of Jiangzhou, Pingyang Prefecture, Shanxi. His courtesy name was Ruxi; he was from Chaoyi County, Shaanxi, and became a tribute student (gongshi) in the renzi year.

Deng Bangji, Instructor at the Confucian School of Mengcheng County, Fengyang Prefecture, Zhili. His courtesy name was Jingqing; he was from Xuwen County, Guangdong, and became a tribute student in the xinyou year.

Li Bangqi, Instructor at the Confucian School of Jimo County, Jiaozhou, Laizhou Prefecture, Shandong. His courtesy name was Zhengfu; he was registered in an officer household of Qingyuan Guard, Guangxi, and was a native of Yishan County. He became a tribute student in the xinyou year.

Wang Yiyue, Instructor at the Confucian School of Xiangcheng County, Xuzhou, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan. His courtesy name was Zhenfu; he was from Lianjiang County, Fujian, and became a tribute student in the wuwu year.

Hou Yiwei, Instructor at the Confucian School of Linzhang County, Zhangde Prefecture, Henan. His courtesy name was Zhiqing; he was from Chang'an County, Shaanxi, and became a tribute student in the wuwu year.

Liu Qifeng, Instructor at the Confucian School of Jiangling County, Jingzhou Prefecture, Huguang. His courtesy name was Yingming; he was from Luzhou, Sichuan, and became a tribute student in the xinyou year.

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
顏淵問仁子曰克己復禮為仁一日克己
復禮天下歸仁焉為仁由己而由人乎
哉顏淵曰請問其目子曰非禮勿視非
禮勿聽非禮勿言非禮勿動顏淵曰回
雖不敏請事斯語矣
詩曰在彼無惡在此無射庶幾夙夜以永
終譽君子未有不如此而蚤有譽於天
===
下者也
敢問何謂浩然之氣曰難言也其為氣也
至大至剛以直養而無害則塞于天地
之間其為氣也配義與道
易
居貞之吉順以從上也
節以制度不傷財不害民
引而伸之觸類而長之天下之能事畢矣
古者包犧氏之王天下也仰則觀象於天
alt_text:
第壹塲
四書
顔淵問仁子曰克己復禮爲仁一日克己
復禮天下歸仁焉爲仁由己而由人乎
哉顔淵曰請問其目子曰非禮勿視非
禮勿聽非禮勿言非禮勿動顔淵曰回
雖不敏請事斯語矣
詩曰在彼無惡在此無射庶幾夙夜以永
終譽君子未有不如此而蚤有譽於天
下者也
===
敢問何謂浩然之氣曰難言也其爲氣也
至大至剛以直養而無害則塞于天地
之間其爲氣也配義與道
易
居貞之吉順以從上也
節以制度不傷財不害民
引而伸之觸類而長之天下之能事畢矣
古者包犧氏之王天下也仰則觀象於天
punctuated:
第壹場

四書

顏淵問仁。子曰：「克己復禮為仁。一日克己復禮，天下歸仁焉。為仁由己，而由人乎哉？」顏淵曰：「請問其目。」子曰：「非禮勿視，非禮勿聽，非禮勿言，非禮勿動。」顏淵曰：「回雖不敏，請事斯語矣。」

詩曰：「在彼無惡，在此無射。庶幾夙夜，以永終譽。」君子未有不如此而蚤有譽於天下者也。

「敢問何謂浩然之氣？」曰：「難言也。其為氣也，至大至剛，以直養而無害，則塞于天地之間。其為氣也，配義與道。」

易

居貞之吉，順以從上也。

節以制度，不傷財，不害民。

引而伸之，觸類而長之，天下之能事畢矣。

古者包犧氏之王天下也，仰則觀象於天
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Yan Yuan asked about benevolence. The Master said: “To restrain oneself and return to ritual propriety is benevolence. If for a single day one restrains oneself and returns to ritual propriety, all under Heaven will acknowledge one’s benevolence. Practicing benevolence depends on oneself. Could it depend on others?” Yan Yuan said: “May I ask for its particulars?” The Master said: “Do not look at what is contrary to ritual propriety; do not listen to what is contrary to ritual propriety; do not speak what is contrary to ritual propriety; do not act contrary to ritual propriety.” Yan Yuan said: “Though I, Hui, am not quick to understand, I beg leave to put these words into practice.”

The Book of Odes says: “There, let there be no hatred; here, let there be no weariness. Strive for this morning and night, that your good reputation may endure forever.” No gentleman has ever gained an early reputation throughout the world without acting in this way.

“May I ask what is meant by the vast, overflowing vital force?” He replied: “It is difficult to describe. As a vital force, it is supremely great and supremely firm. If nourished with uprightness and left unharmed, it fills the space between Heaven and Earth. As a vital force, it accords with righteousness and the Way.”

Book of Changes

The good fortune of remaining steadfast lies in yielding and following those above.

Regulate through institutions and measures, without wasting resources or harming the people.

Draw out and extend these principles; develop them through contact with analogous cases, and all that can be accomplished under Heaven will be encompassed.

In ancient times, when Bao Xi ruled all under Heaven, he looked upward and observed the patterns in Heaven …

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
俯則觀法於地觀鳥獸之文與地之宜
近取諸身遠取諸物於是始作八卦以
通神明之德以類萬物之情
書
臯陶拜手稽首颺言曰念哉率作興事慎
乃憲欽哉屢省乃成欽哉乃賡載歌曰
元首明哉股肱良哉庶事康哉
俾率先王迪我高后以康兆民
不作無益害有益功乃成不貴異物賤用
===

猷則入告爾后于內爾乃順之于外曰
斯謀斯猷惟我后之德
詩
鳲鳩在桑其子在棘淑人君子其儀不忒
其儀不忒正是四國
戎車既駕四牡業業豈敢定居一月三捷
詒厥孫謀以燕翼子

俯則觀法於地，觀鳥獸之文與地之宜，近取諸身，遠取諸物，於是始作八卦，以通神明之德，以類萬物之情。

書
臯陶拜手稽首，颺言曰：「念哉！率作興事，慎乃憲。欽哉！屢省乃成，欽哉！」乃賡載歌曰：「元首明哉！股肱良哉！庶事康哉！」
俾率先王，迪我高后，以康兆民。
不作無益害有益，功乃成；不貴異物賤用物，民乃足。
出入自爾師虞，庶言同則繹。爾有嘉謀嘉猷，則入告爾后于內，爾乃順之于外，曰：「斯謀斯猷，惟我后之德。」

詩
鳲鳩在桑，其子在棘。淑人君子，其儀不忒。其儀不忒，正是四國。
戎車既駕，四牡業業。豈敢定居？一月三捷。
詒厥孫謀，以燕翼子。
translation_en:
…looking down, he observed patterns on the earth. He observed the markings of birds and beasts and the things suited to the land. Near at hand, he drew upon his own body; farther afield, upon other things. Thus he first created the eight trigrams, to comprehend the powers of the divine intelligence and to classify the essential qualities of the myriad things.

Book of Documents
Gao Yao bowed with his hands joined and his forehead to the ground, and proclaimed: “Be mindful! In undertaking work and initiating affairs, be careful of your rules. Be reverent! Repeatedly examine your accomplishments. Be reverent!” Then he continued the song: “When the head is enlightened, the limbs are worthy, and all affairs prosper!”
Cause us to follow the former kings and tread the path of our exalted forebears, thereby bringing peace to the myriad people.
Do not undertake useless things that harm useful endeavors; then your work will succeed. Do not prize exotic things and disdain useful goods; then the people will have enough.
In issuing and receiving commands, consult your colleagues; when their views agree, examine them. If you have good plans and sound counsels, enter and report them to your sovereign within the court; then carry them out outside, saying: “These plans and these counsels are the virtue of our sovereign.”

Book of Odes
The cuckoo is in the mulberry tree; its young are in the thorn trees. The good and noble gentleman is unfailing in his deportment. Unfailing in his deportment, he sets right the states of the four quarters.
The war chariots are harnessed; the four stallions are mighty. How dare we settle down to rest? In one month, three victories!
He bequeathed plans to his descendants, thereby bringing peace to and protecting his children.

translation_en:
…We have set out the clear wine; grant us the fulfillment of our thoughts. There is also harmoniously seasoned broth, prepared and brought into balance. In exchanging toasts [?], there is no speaking; there is no contention. Bless us with long life, with venerable old age without limit. With bound wheel hubs [?] and ornamented crossbars, the eight carriage bells ring out. We approach and present offerings; the mandate we receive is vast and enduring. From Heaven descends well-being, with plentiful harvests in abundant years. Come, draw near and partake; send down blessings without end.

Spring and Autumn Annals

In spring, the Marquis of Teng and the Marquis of Xue came to pay court. 〔Eleventh year of Duke Yin.〕

The armies of Qi, Song, and Cao encamped at Niebei to relieve Xing. 〔First year of Duke Xi.〕

Zhongsun Mie joined Luan Yan of Jin, Hua Yuan of Song, Ning Zhi of Wei, and men of Cao, Ju, Zhu, Teng, and Xue in besieging Pengcheng in Song. In summer, Han Jue of Jin led an army to attack Zheng. Zhongsun Mie joined Cui Zhu of Qi and men of Cao, Zhu, and Qi 杞 in encamping at Zeng. In autumn, Prince Renfu of Chu led an army to invade Song. 〔First year of Duke Xiang.〕

In summer, the duke met the Marquis of Qi at Jiagu. The duke returned from Jiagu. Men of Qi came to return the lands of Yun, Huan, and Guiyin. 〔All in the tenth year of Duke Ding.〕 Shusun Zhouchou led an army to dismantle the fortifications of Hou. Jisun Si and Zhongsun Heji led an army to dismantle the fortifications of Fei. 〔Both in the eleventh year of Duke Ding.〕

無曠土，無游民，食節事時，民咸安其居，樂事勸功，尊君親上，然後興學。

臣下竭力盡能，以立功于國，君必報之以爵祿，故臣下皆務竭力盡能，以立功。是以國安而君寧。禮無不答，言上之不虛取于下也。上必明正道以道民，民道之而有功，然後取其什一，故上用足而下不匱也。是以上下和親而不相怨也。和寧，禮之用也。此君臣上下之大義也。

translation_en:
Let no land lie idle and no people remain without occupation. Let consumption be regulated and labor undertaken at the proper seasons. Once the people are all secure in their dwellings, take pleasure in their work, strive for achievement, honor their ruler, and cherish their superiors, then establish schools.
Thus music is the mandate of Heaven and Earth, the ordering principle of balance and harmony, and something human feelings cannot do without.
To bestow generously and provide everything needed may indeed be called freedom from want.
When subjects exert all their strength and abilities to render service to the state, the ruler must reward them with rank and emoluments. Thus all subjects strive to exert their strength and abilities to render service. In this way the state is secure and the ruler at peace. That ritual allows no act to go unanswered means that those above do not take from those below without giving in return. Those above must make clear the correct Way to guide the people. Only after the people follow it and achieve results do those above take one-tenth of their produce. Thus those above have enough for their expenditures, while those below suffer no shortage. Consequently, those above and below live in harmony and affection, without mutual resentment. Harmony and peace are the effects of ritual. This is the great principle governing ruler and subject, superior and subordinate.

Five topics for legal judgments:
Failure to memorialize on a matter that ought to be reported to the throne.
Assessment of commodity prices by market officials.
Failure to drill soldiers.
Unauthorized levies under the pretext of public business.
Manufacture or construction that does not conform to prescribed standards.

Five policy questions.
Question: The Book of Documents says, “The former kings were able to heed Heaven’s warnings.” The Book of Changes says, “The gentleman, through fear and apprehension, cultivates himself and examines his conduct.” Consider “the great flood warns me” and the self-reproach at the Mulberry Grove: when have emperors and kings ever failed to cultivate virtue in order to turn Heaven’s disposition? We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao received Heaven’s mandate and was especially scrupulous in heeding Heaven’s warnings. In his time, there were edicts soliciting counsel and admonitions to attendant ministers and ministers of the central secretariat. His efforts to cultivate virtue and examine his faults were most thorough. Furthermore…

punctuated: 命儒臣爲《存心》《省躬》二錄，其義何歟？逮我世宗肅皇帝應運中興，日躋聖敬，恒暘則禱，恒雨則禱，所以感格者亦至矣。往聞欽天有頌，星變有勅，昭回雲漢，可得而恭述之歟？仰惟皇上天縱仁明，厲精圖治。邇者日食元正，致厪諭旨；三時不雨，上軫聖衷。畏天一念，質諸皇祖、世宗，無二致者，是宜天休滋至矣。然得之四方，尚有如堯湯之患焉，何歟？抑大小臣工未能敷宣德意致然歟？豈聖政萬分一猶有所未盡歟？諸士幸直言之，執事者願有聞也。
translation_en:
…he commanded his Confucian officials to compile the two records, Preserving the Mind and Examining One’s Conduct. What was the meaning of this? When our Emperor Shizong, posthumously titled Su, responded to Heaven’s appointed course and brought about a restoration, his sagely reverence increased daily. He prayed when sunshine persisted, and prayed when rain persisted: his efforts to move Heaven and secure its response were likewise consummate. We have heard that there was an ode on revering Heaven and an edict concerning celestial anomalies. Their radiance shone across the Milky Way: might you respectfully recount them?
We reverently consider that His Majesty is endowed by Heaven with benevolence and discernment, and devotes his energies to achieving good government. Recently, a solar eclipse on New Year’s Day occasioned his solicitous instruction; the absence of rain for three seasons has troubled his sagely heart. His single-minded reverence for Heaven, measured against that of his imperial ancestor and Shizong, is entirely the same. Thus Heaven’s blessings should surely arrive in increasing abundance. Yet reports from the four quarters still tell of calamities like those of Yao and Tang. Why is this? Could it be that officials, great and small, have failed to give full effect to his virtuous intentions, and thereby brought this about? Could even one ten-thousandth part of his sagely government remain unfulfilled? You scholars are asked to speak frankly; those conducting this examination wish to hear your views.

translation_en:
Question: Sovereigns have long exalted civil education to adorn an age of peace and cultivated military accomplishments to suppress disorder and depredation. The ceremonies for their visits to the schools and the procedures for reviewing troops may be examined and taken as models in the “Protector and Tutor” chapter of the Elder Dai’s Record of Rites and the section on the Grand Minister of War in the Offices of Zhou. Yet visiting the schools is a single activity: why is it variously associated with sacrificial offerings to the sages and teachers, honoring the aged, promulgating music and dances, or inspecting those who fail to follow instruction? Military reviews have established procedures, yet some accounts speak of three hunts each year; others of autumn and winter practice in the five forms of warfare, archery, charioteering, and wrestling; others of mustering troops every three years; and still others of a grand inspection every five years. Does each account have its own grounds?

Confucian scholars all seek reliable evidence in the Rites of Zhou and take their standards of judgment from the Spring and Autumn Annals. Yet the Rites of Zhou survives and says nothing at all about sovereigns visiting the schools; the Spring and Autumn Annals records a grand military review, but its commentary interprets the entry as a criticism. How can this be explained? Rulers of the Han and Tang who aspired to good government sometimes admired and followed these precedents, earning praise in the histories. Yet their government ultimately failed to equal that of antiquity. Why was this?

Our two ancestral founders possessed sagely civil accomplishments and divine martial prowess; their virtue was unsurpassed and their achievements outstanding. Even amid the pressing demands of warfare, they scrupulously observed the ceremonies of visiting the imperial school; while rites and music were newly flourishing, they rigorously maintained the procedures for mustering troops. How lofty and resplendent—nothing could surpass them! Our Emperor has further carried on their achievements and extended their glory. At the very beginning of his reign, he personally visited the Imperial University, and two years later …

問：古者衆建宗藩，填撫王室，所以固磐石之基，為萬世計也。漢初大啟九國，周匝三垂，遂有末大不制之患。及建推恩之策，子弟莫不畢王矣，乃諸侯無擅命之强，大農無詔祿之費，其制可得聞歟？唐自貞觀中，疏屬王者已降為公，其祿甚簡，無庸論已。及宋聚族而養之京師，宋臣以為冗費，熙寧一詔，費遂大省，其何術以救弊歟？

…held a grand review of the garrison troops. His achievements in civil education and military affairs have added lustre to the glorious deeds of his predecessors. Moral instruction should therefore have reached its highest flourishing, and his awe-inspiring prestige should shine resplendently, far surpassing even the Three Dynasties. Yet the practical accomplishments of Confucian learning remain deficient, and military preparations have deteriorated; those who discuss affairs are still apprehensive. Could the true basis on which emperors and kings achieve good government lie elsewhere? Civil affairs and military preparedness are matters to which scholars have long devoted their attention, and which those presiding over this examination are eager to hear discussed. Please explain them in detail.
Question: In antiquity, numerous princely domains were established for members of the imperial clan to safeguard and sustain the royal house, thereby securing a foundation as firm as rock and providing for ten thousand generations. At the beginning of the Han, nine kingdoms were established on a grand scale, extending around three frontiers. This eventually produced the danger of branches growing so powerful that they could no longer be controlled. When the policy of extending imperial favour was instituted, the sons and younger brothers were all made kings. Yet the feudatory lords lacked the power to issue commands on their own authority, and the Chamberlain for the National Treasury incurred no expense for imperially granted stipends [?]. May we hear how this system worked? Under the Tang, from the Zhenguan era onward, kings belonging to distant branches of the imperial clan were reduced to dukes. Their stipends were very modest, and need not be discussed further. Under the Song, members of the imperial clan were gathered together and maintained in the capital. Song officials regarded this as an excessive expense, but a single edict in the Xining era brought a substantial reduction. By what means was this abuse remedied?
Our dynasty investigated antiquity to establish its institutions, enfeoffed the various princes, and fostered harmonious relations among the nine degrees of kinship. All members of the imperial clan old enough to wear ordinary clothing depend upon the state for their maintenance. The favour bestowed upon them has indeed been generous. Now, however, after a long period of peace and harmony, the collateral branches have multiplied daily, numbering more than a hundred times as many as in the Hongwu era. Even exhausting the tax revenues of the realm to support them continually proves insufficient. From where, then, will their stipends…

…from where, then, are these stipends to come? Taxation today has grown no lighter, and government expenditure is no small sum. If we provide their stipends in full, the state suffers still more; if we consider reductions, the imperial clansmen too are already in severe distress. How can we benefit both and relieve them together? None are closer in kinship than the imperial princes, and nothing commands greater reverence than the Ancestral Injunctions. Fiscal officials and advisers have surely deliberated day and night, yet have found no suitable solution. If we now wish faithfully to carry forward the intentions of the sagely founder and fully to appreciate the circumstances of the imperial clan, what measures would be appropriate? You candidates regularly practice reasoned discussion. Since this is among the greatest and most urgent affairs of state, we ask you to consider it together. If you have proposals that can clarify the gradations of affection due to kin and relieve the pressing needs of the common people, be neither vague nor reticent, so that those who guide deliberations on state affairs may adopt them.
Question: Since the Three Dynasties, few have left their mark as men renowned in their age. Yet from the Han down to the present, there have certainly been men whose good reputations were manifest and whose prestige carried weight among both the Chinese and foreign peoples. Let us consider them with you candidates. There was one whose forthright remonstrance became so well known that a powerful feudatory abandoned his rebellious designs; one whose awe-inspiring righteousness finally made a treacherous strongman ashamed of his wicked intentions; one who rode alone into a helmet [?] and secured the obeisance of the Huihe; one who displayed utter sincerity and dispensed with precautions, thereby calming those wavering in their allegiance; one who went out to govern Yan’an, prompting the Xia people to warn one another not to entertain designs upon Yanzhou; one who entered court as chief councillor to the Son of Heaven, prompting the Liao people to admonish one another to take care not to provoke trouble on the frontier; and one who occupied the office of chief councillor, when a northern envoy came to court, reaching the words ‘Le…’ [?]…

…made inquiries [?]. There was one who twice took charge of Daming, before whom the foreign envoys passing back and forth dared not appear without due respect. These several ministers [?] were all what the ancients called outstanding men. Our own dynasty has recruited and welcomed men of reputation and standing; indeed, no few scholars have risen to prominence as the times afforded them opportunities. There is no leisure here to enumerate them individually. There have also been those who, amid the peril and uncertainty of great upheavals, secured affairs within and devised measures for affairs abroad; those who assisted the sun in shining anew [?], advanced worthy men, and supported the heir apparent; those who, after the loss of Hami, issued strategic directions that brought peace to the Western Regions; those who, when Chaoxian requested passage, forestalled others by defeating their schemes, thereby settling the policy of the state; those who regulated the tribute-bearing foreigners, making them obediently heed commands and put away their bows and arrows; and those who administered Yulin, making the enemy bite their fingers and look at one another in dismay, not daring to loose a whistling arrow. Might these men be ranked alongside those several ministers of antiquity? Or do men of ancient and modern times fall short of one another? You students have revered the lofty conduct of earlier worthies for many years. Discuss the ages in which they lived, so that we may see your learning in seeking the friendship of the ancients.

In honoring virtue and requiting merit, the ritual is supremely…

When our Emperor Shizong Su examined antiquity and deliberated on ritual, he made additions and settled the regulations. 成命已頒而當事諸臣統紀漫無定孰何歟
轉弱爲強之道果在是歟夫審憲章考
制度通儒事也諸士宜有槪於中者幸
爲我一指陳之
punctuated: 祖制，收兵權以飭戎務，何歟？近成命已頒，而當事諸臣統紀漫無定執，何歟？轉弱爲强之道，果在是歟？夫審憲章、考制度，通儒事也。諸士宜有慨於中者，幸爲我一指陳之。
translation_en: …the ancestral institutions, concentrating military authority in order to put military affairs in order—why is this? Recently, the imperial command has already been promulgated, yet the officials responsible have no settled principles for command and discipline. Why is this? Does the way to turn weakness into strength truly lie in this? Examining established statutes and investigating institutions are the business of a scholar of broad learning. You candidates must have deeply felt concerns about these matters; please set them forth for me, point by point.

punctuated:
第壹塲

四書

顏淵問仁。子曰：「克己復禮爲仁。一日克己復禮，天下歸仁焉。爲仁由己，而由人乎哉？」顏淵曰：「請問其目。」子曰：「非禮勿視，非禮勿聽，非禮勿言，非禮勿動。」顏淵曰：「回雖不敏，請事斯語矣。」

汪彥冲

同考試官教諭楊批：「意精詞確，格正氣雄，得孔顏問答之旨，宜錄。」

同考試官教諭侯批：「作此長題，類多浮華。此篇簡易精確，義意貫徹，文體之正，獨見於子，宜錄以式時。」

同考試官教諭李批：「不襲陳言，獨出意見，可以式矣。」

同考試官進士劉批：「此題作者，多騁浮詞而忽正意。惟是作說理詳明，造語老健，且前後脉絡貫通，孔顏授受宛然如見。此必心學有得者，錄之。」

考試官修撰申批：「說理明盡，詞復莊雅。」
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Yan Yuan asked about humaneness. The Master said: “To overcome oneself and return to ritual propriety is humaneness. If for a single day one overcomes oneself and returns to ritual propriety, all under Heaven will acknowledge one’s humaneness. Practicing humaneness depends on oneself; could it depend on others?” Yan Yuan said: “May I ask about its particulars?” The Master said: “Look at nothing contrary to ritual propriety; listen to nothing contrary to ritual propriety; say nothing contrary to ritual propriety; make no movement contrary to ritual propriety.” Yan Yuan said: “Though I, Hui, am not quick to understand, allow me to put these words into practice.”

Wang Yanchong

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: “The ideas are refined and the wording precise; the form is correct and the spirit vigorous. It captures the purport of the exchange between Confucius and Yan Yuan. It merits selection.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Hou, Instructor: “Essays on this long topic are generally florid and superficial. This piece is straightforward, refined, and precise, with a consistent meaning throughout. In your work alone is correctness of literary form apparent. It merits selection as a model for writers of our time.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: “It does not repeat stale expressions but offers independent insights. It can serve as a model.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, metropolitan graduate (jinshi): “Those who write on this topic mostly indulge in empty phrasing and neglect its true meaning. This essay alone expounds the principles clearly and fully, with mature and vigorous phrasing. Moreover, its argument is connected throughout, making the transmission of teaching from Confucius to Yan Yuan seem vividly present before our eyes. Its author must have attained an understanding of the learning of the mind. Select it.”

Comment by Examiner Shen, Senior Compiler: “The exposition of principle is clear and exhaustive, and the language is also dignified and elegant.”

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官右諭德丁批典雅
大賢問仁備聞約禮之敎而以爲己任焉夫約
之以禮聖門求仁之要也大賢以爲己任焉其
諸語之而不惰哉且夫仁道之全顏淵已悟於
心齋之後矣至是而以仁問焉問其所以爲仁
也子告之曰仁豈遠乎哉盖仁非心外物也爲
仁者不必求之博也惟克己之私以復乎禮焉
則人心日微道心日著而可以爲仁矣是仁也
心之所同然也有能一日用其力焉而天下莫
===
不與者亦心之所固有也求之由於己焉而非
人所能預者回也爲之其知所自勵乎然理欲
之幾回已判於聽受之餘矣至是而直以條目
請焉將以知所從事也子又告之曰術豈多乎
哉盖視聽言動之非禮即己也其復禮即仁也
惟於非禮勿視勿聽勿言勿動焉則外者不入
內者不出而仁在其中矣所謂天下歸仁歸此
者也所謂爲仁由己爲此者也回也爲之其殆
庶幾乎顏淵承夫子之誘也乃曰回雖不敏請

考試官右諭德丁批：典雅。

大賢問仁，備聞約禮之敎，而以爲己任焉。夫約之以禮，聖門求仁之要也。大賢以爲己任焉，其諸語之而不惰哉！且夫仁道之全，顏淵已悟於心齋之後矣。至是而以仁問焉，問其所以爲仁也。子告之曰：「仁豈遠乎哉？盖仁非心外物也，爲仁者不必求之博也。惟克己之私以復乎禮焉，則人心日微，道心日著，而可以爲仁矣。是仁也，心之所同然也。有能一日用其力焉，而天下莫不與者，亦心之所固有也。求之由於己焉，而非人所能預者。回也爲之，其知所自勵乎！」然理欲之幾，回已判於聽受之餘矣。至是而直以條目請焉，將以知所從事也。子又告之曰：「術豈多乎哉？盖視聽言動之非禮，即己也；其復禮，即仁也。惟於非禮勿視、勿聽、勿言、勿動焉，則外者不入，內者不出，而仁在其中矣。所謂天下歸仁，歸此者也；所謂爲仁由己，爲此者也。回也爲之，其殆庶幾乎！」顏淵承夫子之誘也，乃曰：「回雖不敏，請
translation_en:
Examiner Ding, Right Mentor, comments: “Classical and elegant.”

The great worthy asked about benevolence, heard in full the teaching of restraining oneself through ritual propriety, and took it as his own responsibility. Restraining oneself through ritual propriety is the essential means of seeking benevolence in the sage’s school. The great worthy took this as his own responsibility: was he not one who, when instructed, never grew remiss?

Yan Yuan had already apprehended in his heart the entirety of the Way of benevolence after fasting his mind. When he now asked about benevolence, he was asking how to practice it. The Master told him: “Can benevolence be far away? Benevolence is no thing outside the mind; one who practices it need not seek it far and wide. Simply overcome your selfish desires and return to ritual propriety. Then the human mind will daily recede, the mind of the Way will daily become manifest, and you will be able to practice benevolence. This benevolence is what all hearts alike approve. If someone can devote his efforts to it for a single day, everyone under Heaven will acknowledge him, for it is also inherent in their hearts. Seeking it depends on oneself; it is not something in which others can intervene. Hui, put it into practice! Surely you know how to spur yourself onward!”

Yet Hui, after hearing and receiving this teaching, had already distinguished the subtle boundary between principle and desire. Now he directly requested its specific rules, so that he might know what to undertake. The Master further told him: “Can the methods be many? Seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting contrary to ritual propriety constitute the selfish self; returning to ritual propriety constitutes benevolence. Simply do not look at, listen to, say, or do anything contrary to ritual propriety. Then what is external will not enter, what is internal will not emerge, and benevolence will be present within. When it is said that all under Heaven acknowledge one’s benevolence, this is what they acknowledge. When it is said that practicing benevolence depends on oneself, this is what one practices. Hui, put it into practice! Surely you will come close!”

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
事斯語焉夫不惟曰不敏以示其謙而必曰請
事以致其力由是而竭其才焉將欲罷不能也
自是而不遠復焉將服膺弗失也吁非善學者
其孰能與於斯哉抑此聖學也孔門傳授心法
而淵源於虞廷者也盖求仁執中無二道也克
復精一無二學也勿視聽言動即無稽勿聽弗
詢勿庸之謂也孔顏之問答舜禹之授受有異
致哉甚矣聖門之學之有本也
詩曰在彼無惡在此無射庶幾夙夜以永
===
終譽君子未有不如此而蚤有譽於天
下者也

事斯語焉。夫不惟曰不敏以示其謙，而必曰請事以致其力。由是而竭其才焉，將欲罷不能也；自是而不遠復焉，將服膺弗失也。吁！非善學者，其孰能與於斯哉？抑此聖學也，孔門傳授心法而淵源於虞廷者也。盖求仁、執中，無二道也；克復、精一，無二學也。勿視聽言動，即無稽勿聽、弗詢勿庸之謂也。孔顏之問答，舜禹之授受，有異致哉？甚矣，聖門之學之有本也！

…put these words into practice.” He does not merely say “I am not clever” to show his humility; he also insists on saying “I ask to put them into practice,” thereby committing his full effort. By exhausting his abilities in this way, he will be unable to stop even if he wishes to; by returning before straying far, he will cherish this teaching in his heart and never lose it. Ah! Who but one skilled in learning could attain this? Indeed, this is the learning of the sages: the essential teaching of the mind transmitted in Confucius’s school, whose origins lie in the court of Shun. Seeking humaneness and holding fast to the Mean are not two different Ways; overcoming the self and returning to ritual propriety, and being discerning and single-minded, are not two different disciplines. The injunctions against looking, listening, speaking, or acting contrary to ritual propriety mean precisely: “Do not listen to what has not been verified; do not employ what has not been deliberated upon.” Do the questions and answers of Confucius and Yan Hui differ in their ultimate purport from the transmission between Shun and Yu? How firmly rooted is the learning of the sages’ school!
The Book of Poetry says: “There he is not hated; here he occasions no weariness. May he, from dawn to night, forever preserve his good repute.” Never has a gentleman gained an early reputation throughout the realm without behaving in this way.

… discourse [?] and restore the ancient style. How I admire it, how I admire it!

Examiner Ding, Right Admonisher, comments: “Brilliant and untrammeled.”
The Doctrine of the Mean elaborates upon the Poetry to explain that a true king must obtain renown because he brings his institutions to perfection. When royal institutions attain consummate goodness and an excellent reputation endures without limit, this is no mere stroke of luck. Does examination of the Poetry not make this still more certain? In explaining what it means to occupy a superior position without arrogance, the Doctrine of the Mean reaches this point: the king exercises the three weighty prerogatives above, while the people below are enabled to commit few errors. People know that the king enjoys acclaim, but do they also know whence that acclaim arises? The Poetry says: “There he is not hated; here he is not wearied of.” This speaks of excellent virtue finding acceptance everywhere. “Ever mindful, morning and night, thus forever sustaining his renown.” This speaks of an excellent reputation that never ceases. By examining the Poetry, one comes to understand the way of the king.
The king does not seek acclaim: because the people are enabled to commit few errors, acclaim comes to him. Nor does the world acclaim him out of partiality: because the king alone brings his institutions to perfection, acclaim for him flourishes. Thus, when virtue is complete within himself, and Heaven, Earth, ghosts, and spirits cannot oppose it, there is both consummate beauty and consummate goodness. Wherever the kingly Way reaches, the fame of his virtue shines brightly indeed. Without this, how could he spread such resplendent renown? When his laws suit the people, and neither former kings nor later sages could alter them, they can both extend far and endure long. Wherever the sovereign standard is promulgated, widespread acclaim consequently gathers. Without this, how could he make his brilliant reputation manifest?
There is a Way that can be handed down for ten thousand generations without deterioration. Thus his words and deeds become great models, and his name endures alongside Heaven and Earth: all this arises from that Way. Never has there been one whose transmission and creation of institutions failed to unite discernment and sagacity, yet who possessed …

譽于萬世者也道有放之四海而皆準者故遠
近咸孚而聲施華夏胥此焉未有經濟不本乎
天人而有譽于當世者也借曰有之豈詩人之
旨哉故知詩之所謂終譽則知王者所以有譽
而居上不驕由此其選已雖然王道蕩蕩民無
能名焉而王者何以有譽哉盖不可見者制作
之神可見者經綸之迹知天知人者神也而三

敢問何謂浩然之氣曰難言也其爲氣也

之間其爲氣也配義與道

譽于萬世者也。道有放之四海而皆準者，故遠近咸孚而聲施華夏，胥此焉。未有經濟不本乎天人而有譽于當世者也。借曰有之，豈詩人之旨哉？故知詩之所謂終譽，則知王者所以有譽，而居上不驕，由此其選已。雖然，王道蕩蕩，民無能名焉，而王者何以有譽哉？盖不可見者制作之神，可見者經綸之迹。知天知人者，神也；而三重，迹也。王者感天下以神，而天下囿于其迹，雖譽而不知所以爲譽，此王道之極也。是故堯德如天，而稱之者曰「成功文章」，有以夫！
敢問何謂浩然之氣？曰：「難言也。其爲氣也，至大至剛，以直養而無害，則塞于天地之間。其爲氣也，配義與道。」
張守愚

translation_en:
…and enjoy renown for ten thousand generations. There is a Way that, when applied throughout the Four Seas, proves universally true; it is through this that those far and near alike have confidence, and fame spreads throughout the Chinese realm. Never has anyone enjoyed renown in his own age whose ordering of the world was not rooted in Heaven and humanity. Even supposing there were such a person, could this be what the poet intended? Thus, understanding what the Poetry means by enduring renown, one understands how a king acquires renown; dwelling on high without arrogance, he thereby becomes preeminent. Yet the Kingly Way is so vast that the people cannot find words to describe it. How, then, does a king acquire renown? What cannot be seen is the spiritual efficacy of his creation of institutions; what can be seen is the outward evidence of his ordering of affairs. Understanding Heaven and humanity belongs to that spiritual efficacy; the three weighty matters belong to its outward manifestations. The king moves all under Heaven through spiritual efficacy, but all under Heaven remain confined to its outward manifestations. Although they praise him, they do not know what makes him worthy of praise. This is the highest attainment of the Kingly Way. Thus Yao’s virtue was like Heaven, yet those who praised him spoke of his “accomplished works and splendid cultural forms.” There was reason for this indeed!
“May I ask what is meant by the vast, flowing qi?” He said: “It is difficult to explain. As qi, it is supremely great and supremely firm. If nourished through uprightness and left unharmed, it fills the space between Heaven and Earth. As qi, it accords with righteousness and the Way.”
Zhang Shouyu.
Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor: The vast, flowing qi originates in Heaven and Earth, from which the Way and righteousness issue. Writers generally fail to grasp this. This essay apprehends the principle precisely and incisively, and expounds it almost exhaustively. Its author possesses enduring vast, flowing qi [?] and certainly deserves a high ranking.
Comment by Associate Examiner Deng, Instructor: Its structure and bearing are dignified and imposing; its language and reasoning are integrated and lucid…

The disciple sought to understand qi through words, and the great worthy accordingly showed him the subtleties of its substance and function. How very difficult qi is to express in words! Yet by observing its substance and function, one can assuredly recognize what is called its vast, flowing character. As for qi within a person, expanding it to its fullness depends upon cultivation; making it spiritually efficacious and lucid depends upon the mind. Why was Chou unable to understand this, prompting his question, “What is meant by vast, flowing qi?” It was because he could not grasp the meaning and forget the words, but wished to seek qi through words.

Thus Mencius told him: “Qi is exceedingly difficult to express in words. If I must speak of it, let me speak of its constitution and operation! I have traced this qi to its source, and Heaven and Earth make it clear. Receiving their diffusive qi, one comes to life; its all-embracing expansiveness admits no obstruction—this is indeed greatness in its utmost degree. Receiving their concentrated qi, one comes to life; its stern resolution never bends—this is indeed firmness in its utmost degree. If a person simply nourishes this firmness and greatness with uprightness, without harming it, then its greatness finds its proper embodiment in me, and I shall share the greatness of Heaven and Earth. Its firmness does not depart from my constant nature, and I shall share the firmness of Heaven and Earth. Though this body is tiny within the compass of Heaven above and Earth below, its qi extends boundlessly between them. Such is its constitution.

雖幾微於成性之存而實充周於道義之費其
功用有如此者吁語氣者至此謂之知氣矣凡
有是氣於我者可不求所以善養之哉雖然此
孟子獨得之學也蓋其生世之大敝承道之至
衰其屹然獨立於横流者執極而不變用極而
===
不亂焉何莫非剛大之氣之所顯行哉先儒謂
孟子知言之要知德之奥非苟知之亦允蹈之
嗚呼信矣
易
居貞之吉順以從上也
李廷機
同考試官教諭王 批〔此題人多語意重複此〕
作詞語精粹義理明切盖真有得於絜靜精微之旨者
宜録以式
punctuated:
達也。由是而之焉之謂道，道率乎性，非氣則不行也。人能以其剛大者而配合之，則有以鼓其推行之通，而所以見義必為者胥此矣；有以賛其果决之能，而所以聞道必行者胥此矣。是氣雖幾微於成性之存，而實充周於道義之費，其功用有如此者。吁！語氣者至此，謂之知氣矣。凡有是氣於我者，可不求所以善養之哉？雖然，此孟子獨得之學也。盖其生世之大敝，承道之至衰，其屹然獨立於橫流者，執極而不變，用極而不亂焉，何莫非剛大之氣之所顯行哉？先儒謂孟子知言之要，知德之奧，非苟知之，亦允蹈之。嗚呼！信矣！

易
居貞之吉，順以從上也。
李廷機

同考試官教諭王批：此題人多語意重復，此作詞語精粹，義理明切，盖真有得於潔靜精微之旨者，宜錄以式。
translation_en:
…find expression. To proceed along this course is what is called the Way. The Way follows human nature, but without qi it cannot be put into practice. If one can bring one’s firm and expansive qi into accord with righteousness and the Way, it can stimulate their unimpeded implementation: this is what enables one invariably to act upon seeing what is right. It can assist one’s capacity for decisive action: this is what enables one invariably to put the Way into practice upon hearing it. Although this qi is subtle in its presence within our constituted nature, it fully pervades the extensive workings of the Way and righteousness. Such are its functions and effects. Ah! Someone whose account of qi reaches this point may be said to understand qi. Can any of us who possess this qi fail to seek the means of nourishing it well?

Yet this was a learning that Mencius attained uniquely for himself. He was born into an age of profound corruption and came after the Way had fallen into the deepest decline. He stood alone and unshaken amid the raging currents, holding to the ultimate standard without wavering and applying it without confusion. How could any of this have been other than the manifest operation of his firm and expansive qi? Earlier Confucian scholars said that Mencius understood the essentials of speech and the profundities of virtue; he did not merely understand them, but truly put them into practice. Ah! How true this is!

Book of Changes
“The good fortune of abiding in constancy comes from following those above with compliance.”
Li Tingji

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: On this topic, many writers repeat themselves in both wording and meaning. This composition has refined language and presents its principles clearly and precisely. Its author has indeed grasped the purport of purity, tranquillity, refinement, and subtlety. It should be recorded as a model.

text:
同考試官學正段批任賢養民發明殆盡且
理致渾融辭氣莊重易義之絕佳者
同考試官進士孫批詞氣典雅理致詳明養賢
及民之意發揮殆盡誠深於易者錄之
考試官修撰申批理明詞暢
考試官右諭德丁批精切
大君者逸於任人者也夫任人則裕大君之宜
也六五之養民以之其獲居貞之吉也固其所
哉象傳舉而申之也意謂人君以道濟天下爲
===
極功雖厲精以圖之猶病其施之有未博者頤
之六五曰居貞吉焉則是恭默以待治而天下
自妙于惠德之孚端拱以宅尊而斯世自底于
養恬之域矣果何修而得此哉亦惟其順以從
上耳蓋上九有陽剛之德者也六五以柔居尊

逮矣上之才足以阜成邦國者也于焉篤孚嘉

養有所不贍矣上之賢足以潤澤生民者也于

大君者，逸於任人者也。夫任人則裕，大君之宜也。六五之養民以之，其獲居貞之吉也，固其所哉！象傳舉而申之也。意謂人君以道濟天下爲極功，雖厲精以圖之，猶病其施之有未博者。頤之六五曰：「居貞吉」焉。則是恭默以待治，而天下自妙于惠德之孚；端拱以宅尊，而斯世自底于養恬之域矣。果何修而得此哉？亦惟其順以從上耳。蓋上九有陽剛之德者也，六五以柔居尊，順而從之。蓋知以一人而養天下，吾力有所不逮矣；上之才足以阜成邦國者也，于焉篤孚嘉之道，而日隆夫倚毗之誠。以美利而利萬民，吾養有所不贍矣；上之賢足以潤澤生民者也，于
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Duan, an Instructor, comments: “The appointment of worthy men and the nourishment of the people are elucidated almost exhaustively. Moreover, the reasoning is thoroughly integrated, and the language and tone are dignified. This is an outstanding exposition of the meaning of the Book of Changes.”
Associate Examiner Sun, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi), comments: “The language and tone are elegant and classical, and the reasoning detailed and clear. The meaning of nourishing worthy men so that the benefits reach the people is developed almost exhaustively. This is indeed the work of someone deeply versed in the Book of Changes. Select it for inclusion.”
Examiner Shen, a Senior Compiler, comments: “Clear reasoning and fluent language.”
Examiner Ding, Right Mentor, comments: “Precise and incisive.”
The great ruler achieves ease by entrusting responsibilities to others. Entrusting responsibilities to others brings ample capacity: this is fitting for a great ruler. The six in the fifth place nourishes the people by this means; surely the good fortune it obtains through abiding in constancy is its rightful due! The Commentary on the Images takes up this point and elaborates upon it. Its meaning is that the ruler regards bringing succor to all under Heaven through the Way as his highest achievement. Even when he strives vigorously to accomplish this, he still worries that his beneficence does not extend widely enough. Yet of the six in the fifth place in the hexagram Nourishment, it says: “Abiding in constancy brings good fortune.” Thus, he remains reverent and silent while awaiting good government, and all under Heaven spontaneously experience the wondrous effects of his beneficent virtue inspiring trust. He sits upright with hands folded in his exalted position, and the world of itself reaches a state of peaceful nourishment. What cultivation could have brought him this result? It is simply his compliance in following the one above.
The nine at the top possesses the virtue of yang firmness. The six in the fifth place occupies the exalted position with yieldingness, and compliantly follows it. For he recognizes: “In nourishing all under Heaven as a single person, there are things beyond my strength.” The abilities of the one above suffice to bring the realm to prosperity and fulfillment; therefore, he strengthens his trust and esteem, daily deepening the sincerity of his reliance upon him. “In benefiting the myriad people with splendid benefits, there are needs my nourishment cannot adequately supply.” The worthiness of the one above suffices to bring enriching bounty to the people; therefore …

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
焉勤晋接之交而益切夫忧恂之念用上以敬
下弗計也凡六府之惟修三事之惟和虛已以
聽之而已五之所以恭已而成永賴之功者不
有以哉以貴而下賤勿恤也凡左右有民宣力
四方惟推誠以任之而已五之所以無為而致
容保之治者不有自哉故曰居貞吉也吁若六
五者可謂善用其養者歟雖然順從可也一於
順從而失人主之柄焉不可也皐陶之告舜曰
念哉率作興事慎乃憲欽哉屢省乃成欽哉其
===
意有以識此也是以曰居貞吉又曰不可涉大
川嗚呼聖人之慮審矣
古者包犧氏之王天下也仰則觀象於天
俯則觀法於地觀鳥獸之文與地之宜
近取諸身遠取諸物於是始作八卦以
通神明之德以類萬物之情
袁應祺

焉勤晋接之交，而益切夫忧恂之念。用上以敬下，弗計也。凡六府之惟修、三事之惟和，虛已以聽之而已。五之所以恭已而成永賴之功者，不有以哉？以貴而下賤，勿恤也。凡左右有民、宣力四方，惟推誠以任之而已。五之所以無為而致容保之治者，不有自哉？故曰：「居貞吉也。」吁！若六五者，可謂善用其養者歟！雖然，順從可也，一於順從而失人主之柄焉，不可也。皐陶之告舜曰：「念哉！率作興事，慎乃憲。欽哉！屢省乃成。欽哉！」其意有以識此也。是以曰：「居貞吉。」又曰：「不可涉大川。」嗚呼！聖人之慮審矣！

古者包犧氏之王天下也，仰則觀象於天，俯則觀法於地，觀鳥獸之文與地之宜，近取諸身，遠取諸物，於是始作八卦，以通神明之德，以類萬物之情。

袁應祺

同考試官教諭王批：認理精明，措詞簡切，聖人作易之原，發揮殆盡。後有作者，弗可及已。錄之以式，誰曰不宜？
translation_en:
…thereupon he assiduously cultivates their intercourse through audiences and grows still more earnest in his anxious solicitude [?]. Employing the upper line to show respect for those below, he does not calculate. In all matters concerning the proper management of the six resources and the harmonious conduct of the three affairs, he merely empties himself and listens. Is there not a reason why the fifth line, through reverent self-restraint, achieves results on which people can depend forever? Though exalted, he places himself below the lowly, without misgiving. In assisting the ruler, governing the people, and exerting effort throughout the realm, he merely entrusts responsibilities with complete sincerity. Is there not a source from which the fifth line, without taking action himself, brings about a government that embraces and protects all? Thus it says: “Remaining steadfast brings good fortune.” Ah! May not one such as the six in the fifth place be called skilled in providing nourishment? Nevertheless, following another is permissible; following exclusively, to the point of losing the ruler’s authority, is not. Gao Yao admonished Shun: “Be mindful! Lead the undertaking of affairs; be cautious about your regulations. Be reverent! Repeatedly examine your accomplishments. Be reverent!” His intention was to make this understood. Thus it says, “Remaining steadfast brings good fortune,” but also, “One must not cross the great river.” Ah! How thorough was the sage’s deliberation!

In ancient times, when Bao Xi ruled all under Heaven, he looked upward to observe the images in Heaven and downward to observe the patterns on Earth. He observed the markings of birds and beasts and the suitability of the land. Near at hand he took examples from his own body; farther afield he took examples from things. Thus he first made the eight trigrams, through which to comprehend the potency of spiritual powers and to classify the circumstances of the myriad things.

Yuan Yingqi

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: His understanding of principle is penetrating and clear; his wording concise and apt. He expounds almost exhaustively the grounds on which the sage composed the Book of Changes. Those who write after him will be unable to equal him. Who could say it is inappropriate to include this as a model?

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官學正段批作者類以陰陽消息逐
句發揮殊爲可厭惟此不落俗格而辭簡意足是深於易者
同考試官進士孫批詞簡而意無不虧句古
而理無不徹深得聖人作易之原者宜錄以式
考試官修撰申批敷闡易義殆盡
考試官右諭德丁批峻潔
聖人觀變以立象而有以該微顯之理焉夫陰
陽至變也聖人博觀之以立象而微顯之理焉
有不該者哉大傳推聖人立象之原也意謂易
===
之作也其於隆古乎其當包犧氏之繼天立極
乎然豈以私智創爲者耶盖其聖神之縱於天
者随在以察夫陰陽之端睿智之涵於心者徧
觀以盡夫消息之變有見於在天成象也仰以
觀之而陰陽之經緯者無弗察焉在地效法也
俯以觀之而陰陽之森列者無弗察焉鳥獸之
文天地之宜莫非易也莫非其所觀也近之一
身遠之萬物莫非易也莫非其所取也由是據
其俯仰之所察者而洩之爲竒偶之文即其逺

聖人觀變以立象，而有以該微顯之理焉。夫陰陽至變也，聖人博觀之以立象，而微顯之理焉有不該者哉？大傳推聖人立象之原也，意謂易之作也，其於隆古乎？其當包犧氏之繼天立極乎？然豈以私智創爲者耶？盖其聖神之縱於天者，随在以察夫陰陽之端；睿智之涵於心者，徧觀以盡夫消息之變。有見於在天成象也，仰以觀之，而陰陽之經緯者無弗察焉；在地效法也，俯以觀之，而陰陽之森列者無弗察焉。鳥獸之文，天地之宜，莫非易也，莫非其所觀也；近之一身，遠之萬物，莫非易也，莫非其所取也。由是據其俯仰之所察者，而洩之爲竒偶之文；即其逺
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Duan, an Instructor, comments: Writers generally expound each phrase in terms of the waning and waxing of yin and yang, which is exceedingly tiresome. This answer alone avoids conventional patterns; its language is concise and its meaning complete. Its author understands the Changes deeply.

Associate Examiner Sun, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi), comments: The language is concise, yet none of its meaning is without deficiency [?]; the phrasing is antique, yet no principle remains unexplained. The author has profoundly grasped the origins of the sage’s creation of the Changes. This answer should be recorded as a model.

Examiner Shen, a Compiler, comments: It expounds the meaning of the Changes almost exhaustively.

Examiner Ding, Right Mentor, comments: Lofty and clean in style.

The sage observed transformations to establish images, thereby encompassing the principles of both the hidden and the manifest. Yin and yang are supremely changeable. When the sage observed them comprehensively to establish images, how could any principle, hidden or manifest, fail to be encompassed? The Great Commentary traces the origins of the sage’s establishment of images. Its meaning is this: was the Changes created in high antiquity? Was it when Baoxi succeeded Heaven and established the supreme standard? Yet could he have devised it through his private intelligence alone? His sagely and spiritual powers, bestowed by Heaven, enabled him to discern the beginnings of yin and yang wherever they appeared; the penetrating wisdom harbored in his heart enabled him to observe comprehensively and fully grasp the transformations of waning and waxing. Seeing that images take shape in Heaven, he looked upward to observe them, leaving nothing unexamined in the interweaving of yin and yang. Seeing that patterns are displayed on Earth, he looked downward to observe them, leaving nothing unexamined in the manifold array of yin and yang. The markings of birds and beasts and the fitting dispositions of Heaven and Earth were all manifestations of the Changes; all were objects of his observation. His own body close at hand and the myriad things far away were all manifestations of the Changes; from all he drew. Thus, drawing on what he discerned by looking downward and upward, he expressed it in patterns of odd and even lines; drawing on what he found far away …

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
近之所得者而擬之於形容之似則八卦成列
而易於是乎作矣是以神明之德若至微而難
通者然皆陰陽之理也卦既立矣性命順焉所
謂清通而不可象者不其通一而無二哉萬物
之情若至賾而難類者然皆陰陽之迹也卦既
立矣物宜象焉所謂散殊而不可紀者不其相
似而不違哉吁此象之所由立也而制器者尚
之歟大哉易也斯其至矣雖然羲皇之易心畫
也得意可也泥于象不可也學易者而有得于
===
心焉則八卦未畫而未嘗無也八卦既畫而非
始有也通乎神明而不為深類乎萬物而不為
迹也而先天之易其在是矣噫安得得意忘象

translation_en:
…what he had apprehended close at hand, representing it through likenesses of forms and appearances, the eight trigrams were arrayed, and thus the Changes came into being. The potency of spiritual illumination may seem exceedingly subtle and difficult to comprehend, yet it consists entirely of the principles of yin and yang. Once the trigrams were established, human nature and destiny followed their proper course. That which is described as clear and all-pervading, yet impossible to depict—is it not comprehended in a single unity, without duality? The actual conditions of the myriad things may seem exceedingly intricate and difficult to classify, yet they are all manifestations of yin and yang. Once the trigrams were established, the fitting characteristics of things were represented in images. That which is described as dispersed and diverse, yet impossible to set in order—do not the images resemble it without discrepancy? Ah! This is how the images were established, and why those who fashion implements esteem them. Great indeed is the Changes! Here it reaches its utmost perfection!

Nevertheless, the Changes of the sovereign Fuxi was the delineation of his mind. One should grasp its meaning; one must not cling to its images. If those who study the Changes apprehend it in their minds, they will see that before the eight trigrams were drawn, it had never been absent, and that their being drawn did not mark its first existence. It comprehends spiritual illumination without being abstruse, and corresponds to the myriad things without being confined to their outward manifestations. Herein lies the Changes of Before Heaven. Ah! Where can I find someone who grasps the meaning and forgets the images, with whom I might discuss the Changes?

Book of Documents

Gaoyao bowed with his hands together and knocked his head to the ground. Raising his voice, he said: “Be mindful! When leading undertakings and initiating affairs, be careful about your statutes. Be reverent! Repeatedly examine your accomplishments. Be reverent!” He then continued the song, singing: “When the head is enlightened, and the arms and legs are worthy, all affairs prosper!”

Zhang Shouyu

大臣儆聖君以君道，而發其意于歌焉。甚矣，君道所係之重也！臯陶述以作歌，其旨深哉！昔臯陶將賡喜起之歌，先致責難之意，乃拜手稽首，颺言曰：「勅天要矣，為君實難，而帝可弗念哉？盖君先而臣從，故勸功有道焉。必也總其綱維，而監于成憲，有奮庸以熈帝載也，無聰明以亂舊章也。立治功而存治體，非帝所當敬哉？君逸而臣勞，故課功有道焉。必也察以官成，而核其功實，三載則考績也，四朝則明試也。以治法而維治人，非帝所當敬哉？」斯盖勅天之永圖，明君之能事。臯陶所欲賡歌者，意謂此耳。乃賡載歌曰：

Its expression is poised, orderly, and fluent—something only a person deeply accomplished in self-cultivation could achieve. When he gives expression to his loyalty through effective service in the future, he will surely continue its echoes. Set this as a model [?].

Comment by Associate Examiner Deng, Instructor: He integrates the meaning of the topic and expresses it in ample, measured language. The atmosphere of supreme harmony in a flourishing age is vividly apparent.

A great minister admonishes a sage ruler concerning the way of rulership and expresses his meaning in song. How weighty are the responsibilities bound up with the ruler’s way! Gao Yao expounded them in composing his song: how profound was his intent! Formerly, when Gao Yao was about to answer the song of joyful, vigorous service, he first expressed his intention of holding the ruler to the most demanding standard. He bowed with joined hands, touched his forehead to the ground, and proclaimed: “Attending to Heaven’s charge is essential, and being a ruler is truly difficult. Can the emperor fail to give this thought? The ruler leads and his ministers follow; thus there is a proper way to encourage achievement. He must hold together the guiding principles and take established statutes as his mirror. Let there be vigorous service to advance the emperor’s undertakings, and no cleverness that disrupts the old regulations. To establish the achievements of government while preserving its fundamental order—is this not something the emperor must attend to reverently? The ruler enjoys repose while his ministers labor; thus there is a proper way to assess achievement. He must examine the completed work of offices and verify the substance of their accomplishments. Every three years, performance is evaluated; at the four court audiences, it is clearly tested [?]. To use the laws of government to hold those who govern to their duties—is this not something the emperor must attend to reverently?”

This, then, is the enduring plan for attending to Heaven’s charge and the work in which an enlightened ruler excels. Such was the meaning Gao Yao wished to convey in his answering song. He then continued the song, singing: …

「元首明哉！股肱良哉！庶事康哉！」盖以君為元首，股肱胥則效焉，庶事胥統宗焉，而興事考成既克明矣。吾見智臨百官之上，而惟臣欽若，汝翼汝為，咸奉法而修職也，有弗良哉？神運萬幾之表，而厥績用成，惟修惟和，盖綱舉而目張也，有弗康哉？股肱以元首而良，庶事以元首而康，為元首者如之何弗敬念也？吁！觀臯陶之歌，而責難之義可以深長思矣。嘗觀之，有虞重華濬哲，君不明乎？俊乂在官，臣不良乎？庶績咸熈，事不康乎？乃臯陶矢詩陳謨，惓惓諷戒。古之大臣憂治世而危明主，類如此。後有以豐亨豫大之說誤其君者，能無愧于臯陶之歌？
「出入自爾師，虞庶言同則繹。爾有嘉謀嘉猷，則入告爾后于內，爾乃順之于外，曰：『斯謀斯猷，惟我后之德。』」
賈一鶚

translation_en:
…“When the head is enlightened, the arms and legs are worthy, and all affairs prosper!” For the ruler is the head: the arms and legs all take him as their model, and all affairs find in him their governing center. He has already shown enlightenment in initiating undertakings and assessing their accomplishment. I see his wisdom presiding over the hundred officials: his ministers reverently comply, assisting him and carrying out their duties, all observing the laws and attending to their offices. Could any fail to be worthy? His spirit operates beyond the myriad affairs of government, and their achievements are thereby brought to completion; everything is ordered and harmonious. It is as when the main cord of a net is raised and its meshes spread open. Could anything fail to prosper? The arms and legs become worthy through the head, and all affairs prosper through the head. How, then, could one who serves as the head fail to reflect reverently upon this? Ah! In contemplating Gao Yao’s song, we may ponder deeply and at length the principle of demanding difficult achievements of one’s ruler. Consider the matter: Chonghua of the house of Yu possessed profound wisdom—was the ruler not enlightened? Men of outstanding talent held office—were the ministers not worthy? All achievements flourished—did affairs not prosper? Yet Gao Yao set forth his verse and presented his counsels, earnestly offering admonition through allusion. Thus did the great ministers of antiquity remain anxious amid good government and alert an enlightened ruler to danger. Could those in later ages who misled their rulers with talk of abundance, success, ease, and grandeur feel no shame before Gao Yao’s song?
“When going out and coming in, consult your assembled officers. Consider their various statements; when they agree, pursue the matter further. If you have excellent plans and excellent counsels, enter and report them to your sovereign within the court. Then carry them out outside, saying: ‘These plans and these counsels are solely the virtue of our sovereign.’”
Jia Yi’e.
Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor: “The meaning of this classical passage concerns selecting what is good and attributing goodness to the ruler; its purport is subtle indeed. This composition is fluent in expression and complete in its ideas, revealing a refined understanding of the classic.”

賢王期大臣擇善于人而歸善于君焉。夫善，公天下者也。擇之人而歸諸君，圖政事君之道至矣。成王命君陳，若謂爾之尹茲東郊也，以裁庶政，以毗一人，而可弗由周公之訓乎？以圖政言之，政由俗革，必有廢有興焉，茲國論所由定也。謀在己而不在人，其于政弗克艱矣。必廣諏咨之益，而致反復之詳，問之左右，問之國人，不敢以自用也。及其既協于僉言，而後審之于獨見。眾之所非，思其所為廢焉；眾之所是，思其所為興焉。因革弛張，求底績于修和爾矣。斯則以人之善為己之善，而謀斷其兼資乎！是故大臣之圖政也，無以有己也。以事君言之，言以道接，必有謀有猷焉，茲君德所由成也。善稱己而不稱君，其為臣弗克忠矣。必效責難之義，而攄入告
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Deng, Instructor: In serving their ruler and planning government, ministers must put aside self-regard. This composition alone grasps the principle with genuine precision, penetrating deeply into the meaning of King Cheng’s charge to Jun Chen.
Comment by Examiner Shen, Hanlin Compiler: Fluent and clear, it captures the meaning.
Comment by Examiner Ding, Right Mentor: A work of refined excellence.
The worthy king expected his great ministers to select what was good in others and credit the goodness to their ruler. Goodness is something shared by all under Heaven. To select it from others and credit it to the ruler is the highest fulfillment of the way of planning government and serving one’s sovereign. In charging Jun Chen, King Cheng seemed to say: “You are to govern these eastern suburbs, directing the various affairs of government and assisting the One Man. Can you fail to follow the Duke of Zhou’s instructions?”
As for planning government, administration changes with prevailing customs: some measures must be abolished and others instituted. Through this, the deliberations of the state reach a settled conclusion. If plans come only from oneself and not from others, one fails to treat government as a difficult responsibility. One must draw widely upon the benefits of consultation and examine matters thoroughly and repeatedly, asking those at one’s side and the people of the state, never presuming to act solely on one’s own judgment. Once a proposal accords with the views of all, one must then scrutinize it through one’s own discernment. Consider abolishing what the multitude condemns; consider instituting what the multitude approves. Retaining or reforming, relaxing or tightening measures, one seeks only to achieve results through good order and harmony. This is to make the goodness of others one’s own: does it not draw upon both deliberation and decision? Thus, in planning government, great ministers must put aside self-regard.
As for serving the ruler, when speech brings ruler and minister together through the Way, there must be plans and counsels. Through these the ruler’s virtue is perfected. If a minister claims credit for goodness himself instead of attributing it to his ruler, he fails to be loyal in his service. He must fulfill the duty of demanding difficult things of the ruler and give expression to his sincerity in presenting counsel within the court…

translation_en:
…the sincerity of presenting counsel: to say everything one knows and leave nothing unsaid, daring to conceal nothing. Yet one must not merely correct and remedy faults within the court; one must also support and advance the ruler’s good purposes outside it, treating these excellent plans as our sovereign’s plans and these excellent counsels as our sovereign’s counsels. Carrying forward his influence and spreading his transforming instruction, one seeks only to bring the ruler to sagely illumination. Is this not to attribute one’s own goodness to the ruler, preserving both loyalty and obedience? Thus, in serving his ruler, a great minister must put aside his own self. Ah! Proceeding henceforth with due care for this principle, one’s work as mentor and protector, and one’s loyalty in giving steadfast assistance, would be worthy of the Duke of Zhou. Could this not be called following the instruction well? Alas! When this Way is not understood, those determined to rely on their own judgment do not strive to gather the thoughts of others and thereby broaden the benefits of loyal counsel. At worst, they become arrogantly self-important and say, “Our ruler is incapable.” The Way of the wholly devoted minister has indeed declined. Were King Cheng’s words perhaps intended to admonish later generations? Otherwise, as the poems “Seeking Counsel” (Fang luo) and “Lesser Caution” (Xiao bi) show, King Cheng’s luminous virtue was far-reaching; yet if he wished his ministers to credit the ruler whenever they did good, there would be little chance of avoiding the beginnings of compliant flattery. Thus I say: this was not King Cheng’s intention for himself; it was an admonition to later generations.

Wang Yanchong

觀聖君垂裕之遠而所事者大矣甚矣聖王為
===
萬世計也武之謀及其孫以安其子焉規模亦
弘遠哉宜詩人咏其事也盖曰人君固以光前
為大烈尤以裕後為遠猷嘗觀遷鎬而知武王
之事矣豈為一時計耶盖其聖心之規畫欲以
植不拔之洪基天造之經綸思以垂無疆之大
業其作邑也則前定夫萬世輿圖之固凡周之

邦啟土有以詒之矣其建學也則豫開夫萬年
文教之傳凡周之文孫所以勸學興禮以為天

精切，句句有法，真範世之章也！非邃于詩學者撰不到此。

同考試官教諭李批：詩義類多歸重武王能燕其子，為謀之善，乃其事之大者。不知翼之可子，詩人稱子孫敬以承之也。此作以執競敬勝入講，得之矣，宜錄以式。

考試官右諭德丁批：莊重。

觀聖君垂裕之遠，而所事者大矣。甚矣，聖王為萬世計也！武之謀及其孫，以安其子焉，規模亦弘遠哉！宜詩人咏其事也。盖曰：人君固以光前為大烈，尤以裕後為遠猷。嘗觀遷鎬而知武王之事矣，豈為一時計耶？盖其聖心之規畫，欲以植不拔之洪基；天造之經綸，思以垂無疆之大業。其作邑也，則前定夫萬世輿圖之固，凡周之文孫所以居重馭輕，以為天下觀者，自王之建邦啟土有以詒之矣。其建學也，則豫開夫萬年文教之傳，凡周之文孫所以勸學興禮，以為天
translation_en:
…precise and incisive, with every sentence observing proper method: truly an essay to serve as a model for the age! Someone without profound learning in the Book of Odes could not have composed this.

Associate Examiner Li, an Instructor, comments: Interpretations of this ode generally place the emphasis on King Wu’s ability to bring peace to his son, treating the excellence of his planning as the great achievement in this affair. They fail to understand the phrase concerning aiding his son [?]: the poet speaks of sons and grandsons reverently carrying on what they receive. This essay introduces its exposition through steadfast strength and the predominance of reverence, thereby grasping the meaning. It should be recorded as a model.

Associate Examiner Liu, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi), comments: The topic is apprehended accurately and incisively; the diction is elegant and vigorous. This is an ancient strain within contemporary examination prose. It should be recorded as a model.

Examiner Shen, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: The language and meaning are fully and fluently developed.

Examiner Ding, Right Mentor, comments: Solemn and dignified.

Consider how far into the future a sage ruler bequeaths prosperity: great indeed are the undertakings to which he applies himself. How profoundly the sage king plans for ten thousand generations! King Wu’s planning extended to his grandsons, thereby securing peace for his son. How broad and far-reaching was its scope! It is fitting that the poet should sing of his deeds. For a ruler certainly regards bringing glory to his predecessors as a great achievement, but even more regards providing abundantly for his successors as a far-reaching design. I have considered the removal of the capital to Hao and thereby understood King Wu’s undertakings. Could his plans have been for his own time alone? The designs of his sagely mind sought to establish a vast foundation that could never be uprooted; his ordering of the realm, like Heaven’s work of creation, aimed to bequeath an enterprise without bounds.

In establishing his capital, he secured in advance the territorial stability of ten thousand generations. All the means by which Zhou’s cultivated descendants could occupy the commanding center, govern the dependent regions, and stand as an example for all under Heaven had been bequeathed to them through the king’s founding of the state and opening of its territory. In establishing schools, he opened in advance the transmission of cultural instruction for ten thousand years. All the means by which Zhou’s cultivated descendants could encourage learning and promote ritual, so as to take the lead for all under Heaven…

text:
下先者自王之建國君民有以詒之矣誠如是
也而能敬之子復何爲哉吾知慶流于後裔而
繼王之體者洪圖自得于親承裕及于後昆而
紹王之休者大勳無勞于再集有京師以爲四
方之極而皇靈已張王之子惟穆穆焉循其執
競無競之家法以垂拱于穆清而已矣寧庸于
締造之艱也哉有國學以爲賢士之關而皇風
已暢王之子惟翼翼焉持其敬勝義勝之心法
以恭己於南面而已矣何事于經營之力也哉
===
吁此固武王之所有事也信乎其克君歟抑嘗
觀之郊鄏之鼎成均之制成王周公繼之然後
大備毋乃詒謀燕翼之未盡乎噫毋遠天室營
于洛邑固武王之志也成王特善繼之耳制禮
作樂然後大行周公亦因辟雝之建而潤色之
耳吾於是而益知武王豐芑之仁
既載清酤賚我思成亦有和羹既戒既平
醓假無言時靡有爭綏我眉壽黃耇無
疆約軝錯衡八鸞鶬鶬以假以享我受
