下先者，自王之建國君民有以詒之矣。誠如是也，而能敬之子復何爲哉？吾知慶流于後裔，而繼王之體者，洪圖自得于親承；裕及于後昆，而紹王之休者，大勳無勞于再集。有京師以爲四方之極，而皇靈已張，王之子惟穆穆焉循其執競無競之家法，以垂拱于穆清而已矣，寧庸于締造之艱也哉？有國學以爲賢士之關，而皇風已暢，王之子惟翼翼焉持其敬勝義勝之心法，以恭己於南面而已矣，何事于經營之力也哉？吁！此固武王之所有事也，信乎其克君歟！抑嘗觀之，郊鄏之鼎、成均之制，成王、周公繼之，然後大備，毋乃詒謀燕翼之未盡乎？噫！「毋遠天室」，營于洛邑，固武王之志也，成王特善繼之耳；制禮作樂，然後大行，周公亦因辟雝之建而潤色之耳。吾於是而益知武王豐芑之仁。

既載清酤，賚我思成。亦有和羹，既戒既平。醓假無言，時靡有爭。綏我眉壽，黃耇無疆。約軝錯衡，八鸞鶬鶬。以假以享，我受
translation_en:
…a model for all under Heaven: this, too, was something the king bequeathed to them by founding the state and ruling its people. If this was indeed so, what more remained for a son capable of reverence to do? I know that blessings flowed to later descendants: those who continued the king’s undertaking obtained his grand design directly through inheritance. Abundance extended to succeeding generations: those who carried on the king’s glory had no need to accomplish his great achievements anew. There was a capital serving as the pole toward which the four quarters turned, and royal majesty already prevailed. The king’s son needed only, with solemn dignity, to follow the family precepts of steadfast strength and matchless might, sitting with folded hands in the pure serenity of the court. What need had he to endure the hardships of founding it? There was a state school serving as the gateway for worthy scholars, and the royal influence already spread freely. The king’s son needed only, with vigilant reverence, to uphold the teaching that reverence and righteousness must prevail within the heart, comporting himself respectfully as he faced south upon the throne. What need had he to expend effort on planning and establishing it?

Ah! These were indeed the undertakings of King Wu. Truly, he was capable of being a ruler! Yet consider this: the tripods at Jiaoru and the institutions of the Chengjun academy became fully complete only when King Cheng and the Duke of Zhou carried on his work. Might this suggest that his plans for the security and assistance of his descendants had not been fully realized? Ah! “Do not establish the royal abode far away”: building at Luoyi had always been King Wu’s intention. King Cheng merely carried it forward well. The establishment of rites and creation of music allowed them to come fully into practice; the Duke of Zhou likewise merely elaborated and perfected what the founding of the Biyong royal academy had begun. From this I understand still more deeply King Wu’s benevolence in nurturing future generations, like flourishing millet.

The clear wine has been set out;
grant us the fulfillment of our hopes.
There is also the well-seasoned broth,
prepared and balanced in flavor.
At the presentation of the meat sauce [?], no words are spoken;
there is no contention.
Grant us venerable longevity,
hoary old age without limit.
The wheel hubs are bound, the crossbars ornamented;
the eight carriage bells ring out.
We come forward and offer sacrifice;
I receive…

translation_en:
…the mandate, vast and enduring. From Heaven descends well-being; abundant harvests yield grain in profusion. Come, draw near and partake of the offerings; send down blessings without limit.

Wang Yingxuan

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: The thought is mellow and refined, the diction elegant and vigorous: it sounds exactly like the voice of Tang’s descendant. It should be selected as a model.

Comment by Associate Examiner Hou, Instructor: Among the examination essays interpreting the Hymns, many fail to clarify the relationships between paired ideas, and their flow shifts confusedly. This essay first treats the presentation of offerings as bringing longevity, then treats the receipt of Heaven’s mandate as enabling the worshipper to move the spirits and bring them near. It forms a seamless whole and captures the intention of the original composer. A worthy model indeed!

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: From the preparation of offerings and performance of sacrifice, it traces matters back to gaining the support of Heaven and the people. It grasps the essential meaning.

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, metropolitan graduate (jinshi): Its sympathetic understanding is precise and penetrating, and its writing is brilliant as well. This essay captures the meaning of the Shang people’s sacrifices to their ancestors.

text:
成一代之盛典自今觀之載我清酤祼將行而
□達焉著存之不忘容聲之若接既賚以思
及夫羹定於戒平之後而禮嚴於鬷假之
時穆然無言秩然無爭又何肅敬之至也以一
心之精白主嘉薦之令芳則外盡物而内盡志
焉是以祝告其孝嘏告其慈而神之綏也有慶
眉壽黃耇其永無疆乎然豈予一人之自致哉
覲我羣后車馬盛而大禧承焉軛衡之盡飾八
鸞之和鳴固萃以假饗矣孰知受命既如是其
===
溥將而康年又於是乎迄用四時以和五穀以
昌又何順成之極也以上帝之明賜合萬國之
懽心則百官備而百物具焉是以假之來假饗
之來饗而福之降也無疆人心天命其永有屬
乎然則今之祭固所以纘烈祖之緒而今之福

業之君皆畏天憂人計安萬世而繼統承祧之

translation_en:
…to establish the grand rites of a dynasty. Viewed from the present: our clear sacrificial wine is borne in, and as the libation is about to be performed, it reaches [the spirits?; an illegible character makes the phrase uncertain]. The ancestors’ manifest presence is never forgotten; it is as though one encounters their bearing and hears their voices. The offering has been bestowed with reverent thought. When the soup has been prepared and its flavors balanced, and the rites are solemn as the spirits approach [?], all is reverently silent and orderly, without contention. How consummate this solemn reverence is! With the purity of an undivided heart presiding over the fragrance of the fine offerings, outwardly one provides the material offerings to the fullest, while inwardly one fully expresses one’s devotion. Thus the invocator proclaims the descendant’s filial piety, and the blessing pronounced in reply proclaims the ancestor’s loving kindness. The spirits bring peace and favor: may long life, with aged brows and hoary hair, endure without limit! Yet could I alone have brought this about?

The assembled lords come to pay court to me; their chariots and horses are splendid, and great blessings are received. Their yokes and crossbars are fully adorned, and their eight bells ring in harmony: they have indeed gathered to come and partake of the sacrifice. Who could have known that, with the mandate received so broadly and greatly, years of plenty would also continue to be enjoyed? The four seasons are harmonious and the five grains flourish. How complete this favorable ripening is! Through the manifest gifts of the Lord on High, the joyful hearts of the myriad states are united; all the officers are present, and every offering is supplied. Thus those who approach come to approach, and those who partake come to partake; blessings descend without limit. May the people’s hearts and Heaven’s mandate forever have their rightful allegiance!

Thus today’s sacrifices serve to continue the illustrious ancestor’s legacy, while today’s blessings allow us to inherit his beneficence. How far the blessings of our forebears extend! In general, rulers who found a dynasty all stand in awe of Heaven and care anxiously for the people, planning for the security of ten thousand generations. Yet rulers who succeed to the throne and inherit the ancestral sacrifices carelessly suppose that Heaven and the people can be retained forever. They fail to understand that every portion of wine and every bowl of soup is bestowed by Heaven and supplied by the people, and that in each resides the peace and well-being bequeathed by the illustrious ancestor; these cannot be relied upon forever…

text:
也故保業在于念祖而宗廟之祭繹思尤切焉
言降福而先之以思成商人之意微矣
春秋
齊師宋師曹師次于聶北救邢僖公元年
朱一儒
同考試官進士霍批救邢書次乃責備齊桓
之義此作發揮明切是邃于麟經而有得者錄之
考試官修撰申批就書法立意詞復雅健可錄
考試官右諭德丁批才思超逸
===
伯主恤患而有遺力春秋譏焉此救邢之師當
速故緩桓德之所以爲薄也聞之易曰左次無
咎蓋聖人之慎用兵也乃春秋於聶北之次何
譏乎夫邢以蕞爾之邦而被兵於狄民朝夕急
矣使桓而無意於救邢也救而力不足以存邢
也聶北之次不次無論也今兹爲邢逼狄實關
夷夏盛衰之機而糾宋逹曹又得彼此掎角之
助聶北胡爲乎次哉夫倒懸之勢不可以歲月

…Thus preserving an inherited dominion depends on remembering one’s ancestors, and the sacrifices in the ancestral temple make sustained reflection especially urgent. In speaking of blessings descending, the text first speaks of reflecting on ancestral accomplishments: profound indeed was the intent of the people of Shang.
Spring and Autumn Annals
“The armies of Qi, Song, and Cao encamped at Niebei to rescue Xing.” First year of Duke Xi.
Zhu Yiru
Comment by Associate Examiner Huo, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi): “In recording the rescue of Xing, the text writes ‘encamped’: its meaning is to hold Duke Huan of Qi to the highest standard. This composition develops that meaning clearly and precisely. Its author has studied the Classic of the Qilin deeply and gained insight into it. Include it.”
Comment by Examiner Shen, Compiler: “The argument is grounded in the Annals’ manner of recording events, and the language is also elegant and vigorous. Worth including.”
Comment by Examiner Ding, Right Mentor: “His talent and conception are outstanding.”
When a hegemon relieves distress yet holds some of his strength in reserve, the Spring and Autumn Annals censures him. This army going to rescue Xing ought to have moved swiftly, yet deliberately delayed: this is why Duke Huan’s virtue was deficient. I have heard that the Book of Changes says, “The army encamps to the left; there is no blame.” This surely expresses the sage’s caution in employing troops. Why, then, does the Spring and Autumn Annals censure the encampment at Niebei? Xing was a tiny state suffering attack by the Di, and its people were in peril morning and evening. Had Duke Huan had no intention of rescuing Xing, or had he attempted the rescue but lacked the strength to preserve it, there would be no point in discussing whether or not he encamped at Niebei. Now, however, pressing the Di on Xing’s behalf truly concerned the critical balance between the rise and decline of the non-Chinese peoples and the Chinese states. Moreover, by rallying Song and reaching out to Cao, he had secured their assistance in mutually supporting maneuvers. Why, then, encamp at Niebei? The plight of people hanging upside down cannot await months and years for relief; an enemy whose power is expanding cannot be overawed merely by an advance proclamation of one’s might. Duke Huan’s strength … [?], yet …

text:
智不足以及之非人情也將毋益邢之疾而收
之以示恩乎斯則養亂之隂謀其仁不足懷也
不然將畏師少猶能止桐丘之奔豈以厚集之
旅而不能於一邢哉抑或待狄之敝而乗之以
示威乎斯則詭遇之近功其義不足稱也不然
孤軍深入猶能獻北戎之凱豈以三國之衆而
不能於一狄哉幸而夷儀播遷桓終得以城邢
藉口有如邢不及遷而遂折於狄則聶北之次
終於不前而桓之威德亦安所復施也聖人盖
===
謂兵以救名非左次之時不得與陘亭之役整
兵慎戰者比傳曰三國稱師見兵力之有餘也
聶北之次譏救邢之不速也得聖人之㫖矣雖
然此春秋罪桓也則城邢何以予桓夫保小寡
周道也蠻夷猾夏周禍也天下無王連帥溺其
職矣非桓則尊周攘夷誰耶故簡書是從前乎
美救邢夷儀是遷後乎美城邢明天下不可無
桓也其聖人之微權也夫
仲孫蔑會晉欒黶宋華元衛甯殖曹人莒

punctuated:
智不足以及之，非人情也。將毋益邢之疾，而收之以示恩乎？斯則養亂之隂謀，其仁不足懷也。不然，將畏師少？猶能止桐丘之奔，豈以厚集之旅，而不能於一邢哉？抑或待狄之敝，而乗之以示威乎？斯則詭遇之近功，其義不足稱也。不然，孤軍深入，猶能獻北戎之凱，豈以三國之衆，而不能於一狄哉？幸而夷儀播遷，桓終得以城邢藉口。有如邢不及遷，而遂折於狄，則聶北之次終於不前，而桓之威德亦安所復施也？聖人盖謂兵以救名，非左次之時，不得與陘亭之役整兵慎戰者比。傳曰：「三國稱師，見兵力之有餘也；聶北之次，譏救邢之不速也。」得聖人之㫖矣。
雖然，此春秋罪桓也，則城邢何以予桓？夫保小寡，周道也；蠻夷猾夏，周禍也。天下無王，連帥溺其職矣。非桓，則尊周攘夷誰耶？故簡書是從，前乎美救邢；夷儀是遷，後乎美城邢。明天下不可無桓也，其聖人之微權也夫！
仲孫蔑會晉欒黶、宋華元、衛甯殖、曹人、莒
translation_en:
…yet lacked the wisdom to grasp it—this would be contrary to human nature. Could he have intended to aggravate Xing’s distress and then take it under his protection to display his beneficence? This would be a covert scheme to nurture disorder; such benevolence could not win people’s hearts. Otherwise, was he afraid his troops were too few? He had nevertheless been able to halt the rout at Tongqiu; how could he, with forces assembled in strength, have been unable to save a single state of Xing? Or was he waiting for the Di to become exhausted, then taking advantage of them to display his might? This would be a short-term achievement gained by devious means; its righteousness would not merit praise. Otherwise, even with a lone army penetrating deep into enemy territory, he had been able to report victory over the Northern Rong. How could the forces of three states have been unable to overcome the Di alone? Fortunately, Xing relocated to Yiyi, and Duke Huan ultimately had the building of Xing’s walls as an excuse. Had Xing failed to move in time and consequently fallen to the Di, the encampment at Niebei would have ended without an advance. Where, then, could Huan have exercised his might and beneficence? The Sage presumably meant that, since the army marched in the name of rescue, this was no time to withdraw and encamp. It could not be compared with the campaign at Xingting, when troops were put in order and battle approached cautiously. The commentary says: “The forces of the three states are called ‘armies’ to show that their military strength was more than sufficient. The encampment at Niebei is criticized because the rescue of Xing was not swift.” This captures the Sage’s intent.
Nevertheless, if the Spring and Autumn Annals condemns Huan here, why does it commend him for building Xing’s walls? Protecting the small and weak was the Way of Zhou; the disruption of the Chinese states by the Man and Yi was a calamity for Zhou. All under Heaven lacked a true king, and the regional leaders neglected their duties. If not Huan, who would have honored Zhou and repelled the Yi? Thus, for obeying the written summons, he is praised earlier for rescuing Xing; for the relocation to Yiyi, he is praised later for building Xing’s walls. This makes clear that the realm could not do without Huan. Such, indeed, was the Sage’s subtle weighing of circumstances!
Zhongsun Mie met with Luan Yan of Jin, Hua Yuan of Song, Ning Zhi of Wei, men of Cao, and Ju…

Observe how the Spring and Autumn Annals twice approves punitive action by the hegemon to clarify the fundamental distinction of status, but pointedly suppresses the foreign power’s act of relief to safeguard the great boundary. This shows how strictly the Sage upheld the distinctions between ruler and subject, and between the Yi peoples and the Xia. Hence his particular attention to the use of armed force.
Formerly, when Duke Dao of Jin took the throne, his ambition lay in leadership of the feudal lords. Thus, when he first came to Song’s relief, there was the siege of Pengcheng; when he subsequently attacked Zheng, there was the encampment at Zeng. Chu then invaded Song to relieve Zheng. Their actions as contestants in warfare were alike; why, then, does the Spring and Autumn Annals approve one and disapprove the other?
Speaking from Jin’s side, the distinction between ruler and subject is the fundamental distinction of status throughout the realm. Yu Shi, a subject, rebelled against his ruler, and Chu and Zheng then assisted him. By installing the five grandees and stationing a garrison of three hundred chariots, they evidently intended to overthrow and destroy the ancestral state. If Jin let this pass without punishment, how could it prevail over Chu? Fortunately, Duke Dao had already punished those who fomented disorder…

之人因正其崇亂之黨魚石俘焉徒兵敗焉諸
侯之師次于鄫以待命焉内則宋難以定而專
土者無所容外則楚勢以孤而助逆者不得逞
虞廷五刑之用周官九伐之法盖庶乎其克舉
矣聖人以為是役也乃翦暴鋤兇之舉而春秋
無義戰非所論於此也故特詳之以示予云自
楚言之夷夏天下之大防也楚人以夷猾夏而
鄭又從而附之懷集矢之私恩棄宗盟之舊好
盖將胥中國而夷之矣坐此見伐楚何辭於救
===
乎夫何共也徒知被患者之可憫不知聲罪者
之得宜呂留侵焉犬丘取焉諸侯之師卒釋鄭
以自救焉在宋則為鄭受侮而戚非自貽在鄭
則德楚益深而交以利合無衣偕作之勤四牡
簡書之畏盖不得而藉口矣聖人以為是役也
乃保奸留慝之師而春秋善救兵非所施之此
也故特畧之以示譏云嗟乎外寧内憂士燮所
懼柯陵尋盟晉岌乎失諸侯矣非悼公孰振之
觀其逐不臣者七人任六官于民譽内治既飭

…those who fomented disorder, he then proceeded to punish their supporters. Yu Shi was captured, the infantry defeated, and the armies of the regional lords encamped at Zeng to await orders. Within Song, the troubles were thereby settled, and those who seized territory for themselves had nowhere to find refuge; abroad, Chu was isolated, and those who supported rebellion could not have their way. The application of the five punishments at the court of Shun and the nine grounds for punitive expeditions prescribed in the Offices of Zhou were thus nearly realized. The Sage regarded this campaign as an undertaking to cut down the violent and root out the wicked. The saying that there were no righteous wars in the Spring and Autumn period does not apply here. He therefore recorded it in particular detail to indicate approval.

From Chu’s standpoint, the distinction between the Yi and the Xia was a fundamental boundary of the realm. Chu, a Yi state, disturbed the Xia states, and Zheng in turn attached itself to Chu. Cherishing the private favor of gathering arrows [?], it abandoned its longstanding friendship under the covenant of kindred states, as though intending to turn all the central states into Yi. When Zheng was attacked on this account, what justification could Chu offer for coming to its rescue? Yet Duke Gong understood only that the afflicted deserved pity, and failed to recognize that those proclaiming their crimes were acting rightly. Lü and Liu were invaded, Quanqiu was taken, and the armies of the regional lords finally abandoned Zheng to defend themselves. Song suffered humiliation on Zheng’s account, although it had not brought this distress upon itself; Zheng became ever more grateful to Chu, their alliance being joined by self-interest. They could hardly invoke the readiness to rise together expressed in “No Clothes,” or the awe of written commands associated here with “The Four Stallions” [?]. The Sage regarded this campaign as an army’s effort to protect the treacherous and preserve the wicked. The Spring and Autumn Annals’ approval of armies sent to the rescue does not apply here. He therefore recorded it with particular brevity to indicate censure.

Alas! Peace abroad and trouble at home were what Shi Xie feared. When the covenant was renewed at Keling, Jin was perilously close to losing the allegiance of the regional lords. Who but Duke Dao could have restored it? Consider how he expelled seven men who failed in their duties as subjects and appointed men to the six offices according to their reputation among the people. Once internal government had been put in order…

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
默喻若或詔之矣樂其天地之命乎中和之體
備于人而盡美盡善德所不能兼也樂以養優
柔平中之蘊而飭温文恭敬之容是中和異其
用大樂舉其全條貫兼總若或維之矣樂其中
和之紀乎夫天地中和之道皆人情所寓也樂
以立其命而握其紀矣則踐形盡性有全功而
持情合危之具存焉中正和樂有全體而平情
宣化之資在焉以修内則情有所陶鎔而凡性
之欲罔不中節養人于善而不流者此也以修
===
外則情有所檢制而凡衆之動罔不得宜約人
于正而不過者此也樂其可斯須去乎哉曰人
情之所不能免也如其可免則命孰施之紀孰
定之而情或幾于亂矣先王立為之方以教人
而豈徒耶雖然樂由心生者也人能豫養天命
致其中和然後輔之以樂則内外薰蒸而至德
成此聖人根之性情以立兩儀育萬物者也不
然文采節奏于吾身何預人而不仁如樂何哉
是故君子致樂之道尤當求端于心

punctuated: 默喻，若或詔之矣。樂其天地之命乎！中和之體備于人，而盡美盡善，德所不能兼也。樂以養優柔平中之蘊，而飭温文恭敬之容，是中和異其用，大樂舉其全，條貫兼總，若或維之矣。樂其中和之紀乎！夫天地中和之道，皆人情所寓也。樂以立其命而握其紀矣，則踐形盡性有全功，而持情合危之具存焉；中正和樂有全體，而平情宣化之資在焉。以修内，則情有所陶鎔，而凡性之欲罔不中節，養人于善而不流者此也；以修外，則情有所檢制，而凡衆之動罔不得宜，約人于正而不過者此也。樂其可斯須去乎哉？曰人情之所不能免也。如其可免，則命孰施之，紀孰定之，而情或幾于亂矣。先王立為之方以教人，而豈徒耶？雖然，樂由心生者也。人能豫養天命，致其中和，然後輔之以樂，則内外薰蒸而至德成。此聖人根之性情，以立兩儀、育萬物者也。不然，文采節奏于吾身何預？人而不仁，如樂何哉？是故君子致樂之道，尤當求端于心。
translation_en:
…is tacitly apprehended, as though something were imparting instruction. Is not music the mandate of Heaven and Earth! The substance of equilibrium and harmony is fully present in human beings, yet consummate beauty and consummate goodness cannot both be achieved through virtue alone. Music nurtures the inward qualities of gentleness, ease, balance, and centeredness, and orders the outward bearing of refinement and reverence. Thus, while equilibrium and harmony differ in their operation, great music brings forth their entirety, comprehending all their connecting threads, as though something were holding them together. Is not music the ordering principle of equilibrium and harmony!

The ways of Heaven and Earth, equilibrium and harmony, are all where human feelings reside. Once music establishes their mandate and grasps their ordering principle, the work of fulfilling one’s bodily form and fully realizing one’s nature is complete, and the means of sustaining the feelings and bringing peril into accord [?] are present. Centrality, correctness, harmony, and joy are fully embodied, and the resources for calming the feelings and spreading moral transformation are at hand. When used to cultivate the inner self, music molds the feelings so that every desire arising from one’s nature accords with its proper measure: this is how it nurtures people in goodness without letting them drift astray. When used to cultivate outward conduct, music restrains the feelings so that every action of the multitude is fitting: this is how it confines people to correctness without letting them transgress. Can music be dispensed with even for a moment? It is said to be something human feelings cannot do without. If it could be dispensed with, who would put that mandate into effect, and who would establish that ordering principle? The feelings might then approach disorder. Was it to no purpose that the former kings established methods for music and used them to teach the people?

Nevertheless, music arises from the heart. If people can first nurture what Heaven has mandated and bring their equilibrium and harmony to fulfillment, and then supplement these with music, its influence will permeate both inner life and outward conduct, and consummate virtue will be achieved. This is how the sage, taking human nature and feelings as the root, establishes the Two Modes—Heaven and Earth—and nurtures the myriad things. Otherwise, what have ornamental display and measured rhythms to do with oneself? If a person lacks benevolence, what can he do with music? Thus, in the gentleman’s way of bringing music to fulfillment, he must above all seek its beginning in the heart.

尊為天子而宗廟饗之之意是作獨為得之至發揮不匱處
藹然純孝之心溢於言外可愛可傳
考試官修撰申批舂容有致可式
考試官右諭德丁批筆鋒勁健
記者指尊親之事而著其為大孝焉夫尊親之
至莫大乎以天下享也其斯為大孝之實哉是
宜記者引言之也意謂人子有無窮之心而恒
制於有限之分欲其不匱也難矣其惟天子乎
盖其德教之洋溢以溥之則周於萬姓也而懷
其德者胥有以致其方物之陳惠澤之敷施以
推之則刑于四海也而濡其化者均有以畢其
任土之獻一人之孝享羣后之職貢存焉盡天
地之所有者莫不咸在也九重之殷薦百辟之
裸將寓焉極覆載之所通者莫不畢至也如是
非所謂不匱乎盖用力以為孝者心固以力而

translation_en:
“Bestowing widely and providing all things, he may be said to be inexhaustible.”
Chen Shi
Associate Examiner Qian, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi), comments: “‘Bestowing widely and providing all things’ conveys the idea that, a sage in virtue and the Son of Heaven in exalted position, he makes offerings in the ancestral temple. This composition alone truly grasps it. Where it develops the meaning of ‘inexhaustible,’ a warm spirit of pure filial devotion overflows beyond the words. It deserves to be cherished and handed down.”
Examiner Shen, Senior Compiler, comments: “Measured and expansive, with elegance; worthy of emulation.”
Examiner Ding, Right Mentor, comments: “The writing is vigorous and forceful.”
The recorder points to the act of honoring one’s parents and makes clear that it constitutes great filial piety. In honoring one’s parents to the utmost, nothing surpasses making offerings to them with the resources of the whole realm. Is this not the substance of great filial piety? It is fitting, then, that the recorder should cite these words. Their meaning is that a son’s devotion knows no bounds, yet is constantly constrained by the limits of his allotted station. How difficult it is for his provision never to run short! Surely only the Son of Heaven can achieve this!
For his moral instruction overflows: spread abroad, it reaches all the myriad families, and those who cherish his virtue all have the means to present the products of their regions. His beneficence is widely bestowed: extended outward, it serves as a model throughout the Four Seas, and those steeped in his transforming influence all have the means to fulfill their offerings of tribute assessed according to their lands. The filial offerings of the One Man incorporate the prescribed tribute of the many lords; nothing that Heaven and Earth possess is absent. The abundant offerings from the palace’s ninefold enclosure embody the libation service of the hundred lords; everything within the reach of Heaven’s covering and Earth’s support arrives in full. Is this not what is meant by ‘inexhaustible’?
For those who practice filial piety through their own strength, their devotion indeed, through that strength…

text:
盡也力所不及吾見其匱矣用勞以爲孝者心
固以勞而盡也勞所不及吾見其匱矣茲則合
四方之貢以寧其神而所以成多儀之享者不
阻於心思之未遂萃九州之美以隆其報而所

punctuated:
盡也。力所不及，吾見其匱矣。用勞以爲孝者，心固以勞而盡也；勞所不及，吾見其匱矣。茲則合四方之貢以寧其神，而所以成多儀之享者，不阻於心思之未遂；萃九州之美以隆其報，而所以昭祀事之明者，不限於分量之有裁。上不愛其德，則下不愛其情，而致敬發情之誠，至是無餘𢢽也。不以天下儉其親，而以天下成其享，追養繼孝之志，至是無遺憾也。此之謂不匱，此之謂大孝矣。吁！非天子，其孰能致之？雖然，孝固以備物爲大矣，亦不必備物而後爲孝也。如必備物而後可以爲孝，則孝爲絕德矣。故尊爲天子，孝也；耕于歷山，亦孝也。使側陋莫揚，舜將不得稱終身慕乎？故曰：「因心之謂孝。」

第貳場
論
人君動必有所畏
李廷機
同考試官教諭王批〔以所畏而統歸於心，既得要〕
translation_en:
…is fully expressed. Where physical strength cannot reach, I see that it falls short. For those who practice filial devotion through toil, their hearts are indeed fully expressed through that toil; yet where toil cannot reach, I see that it falls short. Here, however, tribute from the four quarters is assembled to bring repose to the ancestral spirits: the provision of offerings in their manifold forms is not obstructed by intentions left unfulfilled. The finest products of the Nine Provinces are gathered to make the repayment of ancestral kindness abundant: the splendor of the sacrificial rites is not constrained by the limits of allotted resources. When the ruler does not stint his virtue, those below do not stint their affection; the sincerity with which reverence is offered and affection expressed thus leaves no regret [?]. He does not, while possessing all under Heaven, stint his parents, but uses all under Heaven to complete their offerings. His resolve to continue nourishing them after death and perpetuate his filial service thus leaves no regret. This is what is meant by never falling short; this is what is meant by great filial devotion. Ah! Who but the Son of Heaven could achieve it?

Nevertheless, although filial devotion finds greatness in the full provision of offerings, it need not await that full provision before it counts as filial devotion. If one could practice filial devotion only after providing everything, filial devotion would become an unattainable virtue. Thus, occupying the exalted position of Son of Heaven is filial devotion; plowing at Lishan is also filial devotion. Had Shun remained obscure and humble, never raised to prominence, could he not still have been said to cherish his parents throughout his life? Hence the saying: “What proceeds from the heart is called filial devotion.”

Second Session
Discourse
“A Ruler Must Have Something to Fear in Every Action”
Li Tingji

Comment by Associate Examiner Duan, School Instructor: He elucidates the meaning of apprehension in action with subtlety and thoroughness, and his language is exceptionally refined. This can indeed serve as a model.

Comment by Associate Examiner Sun, metropolitan graduate (jinshi): The argument is refined, and its exposition clear and exhaustive. He truly understands the foundation of abundant virtue. Select it.

Comment by Examiner Shen, Senior Compiler: He brings out the reverence through which the ruler governs his mind. His ideas are upright, his language dignified, and his exposition methodical. He is a scholar of cultivated character. Accept it.

Comment by Examiner Ding, Right Admonisher: The ability to restrain oneself and remain apprehensive is an abundant virtue in a ruler. This composition expounds it exhaustively in all its subtleties. It should be selected as a model.

There is no other reason why a ruler can occupy the imperial throne without a troubled conscience: it is simply that his mind is wholly devoted to reverence. Why is this? The ruler’s mind is the pivot of all transformations and the root of good government; reverence, in turn, is what controls that pivot and establishes that root. Only when the ruler governs his mind through reverence will each and every action of the multitude accord with what is fitting [?], and the proper principles of all under Heaven be realized. Emperors and kings establish their position within this order because they possess this capacity. Without the most abundant virtue, who could attain this? To act otherwise is for a single man to behave wantonly above the people, giving free rein to his excesses and indolence, and thereby abandoning the nature bestowed by Heaven …

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
地之性天下之大可畏者至矣嗚呼弗畏入畏
可不審歟宋儒范祖禹曰人君動必有所畏盛
德也誠知德之言乎請申其說嘗觀天生民而
立之君也則必正之以首出庶物之位焉隆之
以錦衣玉食之養焉予之以宰制萬物之權焉
是故以統馭百官而罔不承式也以臣妾億兆
而罔不從乂也以斂財致用而罔不輸貢也以
詰姦刑暴而罔不咸服也以平邦國征不庭而
罔不震疊也其總攬乾綱役使羣動也若執樞
===
以運之惟吾之闔闢弛張而莫敢違也若持衡
以平之惟吾之調停均節而莫敢抗也故擬其
尊者則曰如天矣語其威者則曰如雷霆矣仰
之則如日月敬之則如神明矣何莫非天之所
畀哉而世主之自恃其崇高者必曰天生德於
予也其如予何哉於是乎有恒舞于宮酣歌于
室者有殉于貨色恒于遊畋者有侮聖言逆忠
直遠耆比頑蹈于夬履之厲者訑訑然曰吾可
以優游逸豫而肆志于萬民之上也而曷畏哉

punctuated: 地之性，天下之大可畏者至矣。嗚呼！弗畏入畏，可不審歟？宋儒范祖禹曰：「人君動必有所畏，盛德也。」誠知德之言乎！請申其說。嘗觀天生民而立之君也，則必正之以首出庶物之位焉，隆之以錦衣玉食之養焉，予之以宰制萬物之權焉。是故以統馭百官而罔不承式也，以臣妾億兆而罔不從乂也，以斂財致用而罔不輸貢也，以詰姦刑暴而罔不咸服也，以平邦國征不庭而罔不震疊也。其總攬乾綱、役使羣動也，若執樞以運之，惟吾之闔闢弛張而莫敢違也；若持衡以平之，惟吾之調停均節而莫敢抗也。故擬其尊者則曰如天矣，語其威者則曰如雷霆矣，仰之則如日月，敬之則如神明矣。何莫非天之所畀哉？而世主之自恃其崇高者必曰：「天生德於予也，其如予何哉？」於是乎有恒舞于宮、酣歌于室者，有殉于貨色、恒于遊畋者，有侮聖言、逆忠直、遠耆比頑、蹈于夬履之厲者，訑訑然曰：「吾可以優游逸豫而肆志于萬民之上也，而曷畏哉？」
translation_en:
…the nature bestowed by Heaven and Earth, then the gravest dangers under Heaven will arrive. Alas! By failing to fear, one enters into what is fearful: can this go unexamined? The Song Confucian scholar Fan Zuyu said, “For a ruler to have something he fears whenever he acts is consummate virtue.” These are indeed the words of one who understands virtue! Allow me to expand upon his explanation.

I have observed that when Heaven brings forth the people and establishes a ruler over them, it duly places him in a position foremost among all beings, exalts him with the sustenance of brocade robes and exquisite food, and grants him authority to govern all things. Thus, when he commands the hundred officials, none fails to observe his rules; when he makes the multitudes his subjects and servants, none fails to submit to his government; when he gathers wealth for use, none fails to deliver tribute; when he investigates wrongdoing and punishes violence, all submit; and when he pacifies the states and campaigns against those who refuse to attend his court, none fails to tremble in awe. In his comprehensive grasp of sovereign authority and his direction of every activity, he is like someone operating a pivot: everything opens or closes, slackens or tightens, solely at his bidding, and none dares disobey. He is like someone holding a balance to bring things into equilibrium: everything is adjusted and apportioned solely at his bidding, and none dares resist. Thus, those who seek a likeness for his exalted standing call it Heaven-like; those who speak of his might liken it to thunder. They look up to him as to the sun and moon and revere him as a divine being. What among these things is not Heaven’s gift?

Yet rulers who rely presumptuously upon their exalted standing invariably say, “Heaven has engendered virtue in me; what can anyone do to me?” Thus there are those who dance incessantly in their palaces and sing drunkenly in their chambers; those who give themselves over to wealth and sexual pleasure and spend their days roaming and hunting; and those who scorn the words of sages, oppose the loyal and upright, shun the elders and associate with the obstinate, and tread into the danger of resolute advance. Smugly they declare, “I may idle at ease, indulge in pleasures, and give free rein to my desires above the myriad people. What have I to fear?”

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
自小人之視其崇高而獻諛者亦必曰巍巍乎
唯君爲大天下所望而震焉者也是所畏也非
畏人者也於是有謂豐亨豫大者有謂世已太
平胡爲不樂者有謂天變不足畏人言不足恤
者而曷畏哉是皆言乎無所用其畏也而何以
曰動必有所畏耶噫爲此說者盖未知崇高之
位庸主之所恃以爲安而盛德之君則視之以
爲危也錦衣玉食庸主之所溺以爲豫而盛德
之君則懍懍危懼有天下而不與者也盖嘗蚤
===
夜以思曰天之寵綏我者其責望我者也代理
之未盡吾懼焉若之何其不恐而畏耶其心固
惕然曰一念不謹似無傷也而四海之憂自我
貽焉何可以不畏也一日不謹似無害也而千
百年之患自我致焉何可以不畏也故不敢以
易心乘之也於是乎有朽索之馭焉有虎尾之
履焉有深淵之懼焉不敢以怠心乘之也於是
有刀劔戶牖之銘焉有几席觴豆之銘焉有鍾
皷鐸鞀之設焉不敢以狎心乘之也於是出入

自小人之視其崇高而獻諛者亦必曰巍巍乎
唯君爲大天下所望而震焉者也是所畏也非
畏人者也於是有謂豐亨豫大者有謂世已太
平胡爲不樂者有謂天變不足畏人言不足恤
者而曷畏哉是皆言乎無所用其畏也而何以
曰動必有所畏耶噫爲此說者盖未知崇高之
位庸主之所恃以爲安而盛德之君則視之以
爲危也錦衣玉食庸主之所溺以爲豫而盛德
之君則懔懔危懼有天下而不與者也盖嘗蚤
夜以思曰天之寵綏我者其責望我者也代理
===
之未盡吾懼焉若之何其不恐而畏耶其心固
惕然曰一念不謹似無傷也而四海之憂自我
貽焉何可以不畏也一日不謹似無害也而千
百年之患自我致焉何可以不畏也故不敢以
易心乗之也於是乎有朽索之馭焉有虎尾之
履焉有深淵之懼焉不敢以怠心乗之也於是
有刀劍戶牖之銘焉有几席觴豆之銘焉有鍾
鼓鐸鞀之設焉不敢以狎心乗之也於是出入
punctuated: 自小人之視其崇高而獻諛者，亦必曰：「巍巍乎！唯君爲大，天下所望而震焉者也。是所畏也，非畏人者也。」於是有謂豐亨豫大者，有謂世已太平胡爲不樂者，有謂天變不足畏、人言不足恤者，而曷畏哉？是皆言乎無所用其畏也，而何以曰動必有所畏耶？噫！爲此說者，盖未知崇高之位，庸主之所恃以爲安，而盛德之君則視之以爲危也；錦衣玉食，庸主之所溺以爲豫，而盛德之君則懍懍危懼，有天下而不與者也。盖嘗蚤夜以思曰：「天之寵綏我者，其責望我者也。代理之未盡，吾懼焉，若之何其不恐而畏耶？」其心固惕然曰：「一念不謹，似無傷也，而四海之憂自我貽焉，何可以不畏也？一日不謹，似無害也，而千百年之患自我致焉，何可以不畏也？」故不敢以易心乘之也，於是乎有朽索之馭焉，有虎尾之履焉，有深淵之懼焉；不敢以怠心乘之也，於是有刀劔戶牖之銘焉，有几席觴豆之銘焉，有鍾皷鐸鞀之設焉；不敢以狎心乘之也，於是出入
translation_en:
Petty men who behold the ruler’s exalted position and offer flattery invariably say: “How lofty! Only our lord is great; all under Heaven look up to him and tremble. He is one to be feared, not one who fears others.” Thus some speak of abundance, prosperity, ease, and grandeur; some say, “The world is already at peace—why not enjoy yourself?”; and some say, “Heavenly portents need not be feared, and people’s words need not cause concern.” What, then, is there to fear? All these claims hold that there is no occasion for fear. How, then, can one say that in every action there must be something to fear?

Alas! Those who make such claims do not understand that an exalted position, which a mediocre ruler relies upon for security, is regarded as perilous by a ruler of consummate virtue. Embroidered robes and exquisite food, in which a mediocre ruler indulges for pleasure, leave a ruler of consummate virtue trembling with apprehension: he possesses all under Heaven yet takes no part in its enjoyments. Morning and night he reflects: “Heaven’s favor and protection carry expectations and demands upon me. I fear that I have not fully discharged my task of governing on its behalf. How could I fail to feel apprehension and awe?” His heart remains vigilant, saying: “A single careless thought may seem to do no damage, yet through me it may bequeath sorrow to all within the Four Seas. How could I not be afraid? A single day of carelessness may seem harmless, yet through me it may bring calamity lasting hundreds or thousands of years. How could I not be afraid?”

Thus he dares not occupy his position with a heedless heart. He feels as though driving with rotten reins, treading on a tiger’s tail, or standing in dread before a deep abyss. He dares not occupy it with an indolent heart. Thus there are admonitory inscriptions on knives and swords, doors and windows; inscriptions on tables and mats, drinking cups and food vessels; and bells, drums, clapper bells, and pellet drums set out to sound admonitions. He dares not occupy it with a complacent heart. Thus, in going out and coming in…

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
起居之必欽焉發號施令之必臧焉侍御僕從
之必以正焉不但是也畏其有怠時也於是朝
日以祖識乎地德日中以宣序乎民事夕月以
糾虔夫天刑日入以監九御使潔奉禘郊之粢
盛所以謹其豫怠者無弗至也畏其有怠事也
於是在輿有旅賁之規位宁有官師之典倚几
有訓誦之諫居寢有瞽御之箴臨事有瞽史之
道宴居有工師之誦而又女史授環彤管記過
所以謹其慆淫者無弗至也畏其有怠幾也於
===
是虞賓在位三恪助祭夏士在庭殷士在廟蠻
民在甸夷隸在門所以謹其危亡者無弗至也
不但已也天災雖已銷息矣而及爾出往及爾
游衍所以勅天命謹時幾者無敢肆也祖烈雖
已憲章矣而無作聰明無有辯言所以繼其志
述其事者無敢肆也賢才雖已舉用矣而以敬
大臣以體羣臣所以憂驩兜畏巧言者無敢肆
也四海雖已無虞矣而視民如傷顧畏民碞所
以憂困窮懷勝予者無敢肆也四夷雖已賓貢

punctuated:
起居之必欽焉，發號施令之必臧焉，侍御僕從之必以正焉。不但是也，畏其有怠時也，於是朝日以祖識乎地德，日中以宣序乎民事，夕月以糾虔夫天刑，日入以監九御，使潔奉禘郊之粢盛，所以謹其豫怠者無弗至也。畏其有怠事也，於是在輿有旅賁之規，位宁有官師之典，倚几有訓誦之諫，居寢有瞽御之箴，臨事有瞽史之道，宴居有工師之誦，而又女史授環，彤管記過，所以謹其慆淫者無弗至也。畏其有怠幾也，於是虞賓在位，三恪助祭，夏士在庭，殷士在廟，蠻民在甸，夷隸在門，所以謹其危亡者無弗至也。
不但已也，天災雖已銷息矣，而及爾出往，及爾游衍，所以勅天命、謹時幾者無敢肆也。祖烈雖已憲章矣，而無作聰明，無有辯言，所以繼其志、述其事者無敢肆也。賢才雖已舉用矣，而以敬大臣，以體羣臣，所以憂驩兜、畏巧言者無敢肆也。四海雖已無虞矣，而視民如傷，顧畏民碞，所以憂困窮、懷勝予者無敢肆也。四夷雖已賓貢
translation_en:
…he must be reverent in rising and resting, good in issuing commands and decrees, and upright in his choice of attendants and servants. Nor is this all. Fearing that there might be times when he grows negligent, at morning sunlight he acknowledges the virtues of the earth [?]; at midday he sets the people’s affairs in order; at evening moonrise he reverently attends to Heaven’s laws; and at sunset he oversees the nine ranks of palace women, having them offer in purity the sacrificial grain for the di ancestral sacrifice and the suburban sacrifice to Heaven. He thus takes every possible precaution against ease and negligence. Fearing that there might be matters in which he grows negligent, in his carriage he receives admonitions from the valiant guards; at his station before the palace gate, established guidance from the officials; when leaning on his armrest, remonstrances recited for his instruction; in his sleeping chamber, admonitions from blind attendants; when conducting affairs, guidance from blind musicians and scribes; and in private repose, recitations from the master musicians. Moreover, the female scribes distribute rings to regulate attendance upon him and record his faults with vermilion writing brushes. He thus takes every possible precaution against excess and indulgence. Fearing negligence at the first stirrings of events, he has the descendant of the Yu house present in the honored position of a guest, the descendants of three former ruling houses assisting at sacrifices, men of Xia in the court, men of Yin in the ancestral temple, Man people in the royal domain, and Yi bondservants at the gates. He thus takes every possible precaution against danger and ruin.
Nor does it end here. Though Heaven-sent calamities have already subsided, he remains watchful ‘when you go forth’ and ‘when you wander at leisure’: in reverently attending to Heaven’s Mandate and carefully observing the incipient changes of the times, he dares allow himself no license. Though he has already taken his ancestors’ glorious achievements as his model, he observes the injunctions ‘Do not make a display of cleverness’ and ‘Do not offer specious arguments’: in carrying on their intentions and continuing their undertakings, he dares allow himself no license. Though worthy and talented men have already been promoted and employed, he honors the great ministers and treats the assembled officials with sympathetic consideration: in guarding against men like Huan Dou and fearing crafty speech, he dares allow himself no license. Though all within the Four Seas is already free from danger, he regards the people as though they were wounded and remains mindful and fearful of their formidable power: in caring for those in distress and cherishing those who surpass him, he dares allow himself no license. Though the peoples of the four outer regions have already come as guests bearing tribute…

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
矣而不寶遠物不貴異物所以戒怠荒慎修德
者無敢肆也皇皇焉何動而非畏耶是非不知
天下之莫予違而可以無忌憚也其心固曰天
之所以畀我者非與以可安之地而娛之也誠
遺之以至大而投之以至艱也一念肆則動罔
弗愆將譴告至焉甚者天禄終焉若之何其不
恐而畏耶甚矣盛德之君動必有所畏也稽古
在昔德廣運矣而欽若敬授堯之所爲兢兢也
德罔愆矣而咨岳咨牧舜之所爲業業也文命
敷矣而祗德克艱禹之所爲孜孜也德懋昭矣
而不邇不殖湯之所爲慄慄也萬民咸和四海
永清治已至矣而不遑暇食敬勝義勝文武之
所以翼翼執競也何莫非盛德之至哉然則帝
王之所以熈洪號于無窮者固惟一敬以得之
者也彼有爲昏迷不恭者怠棄三正者狎侮五
常怠荒弗敬者何惑乎安其所危而不自知耶
嗚呼克畏則聖弗畏則狂克畏則治弗畏則亂
其機如此有天下者曷其奈何弗敬

punctuated: 矣，而不寶遠物，不貴異物，所以戒怠荒、慎修德者，無敢肆也。皇皇焉，何動而非畏耶？是非不知天下之莫予違，而可以無忌憚也。其心固曰：「天之所以畀我者，非與以可安之地而娛之也，誠遺之以至大而投之以至艱也。一念肆，則動罔弗愆，將譴告至焉，甚者天禄終焉。若之何其不恐而畏耶？」甚矣，盛德之君，動必有所畏也！稽古在昔，德廣運矣，而欽若敬授，堯之所爲兢兢也；德罔愆矣，而咨岳咨牧，舜之所爲業業也；文命敷矣，而祗德克艱，禹之所爲孜孜也；德懋昭矣，而不邇不殖，湯之所爲慄慄也；萬民咸和，四海永清，治已至矣，而不遑暇食，敬勝義勝，文武之所以翼翼執競也。何莫非盛德之至哉？然則帝王之所以熈洪號于無窮者，固惟一敬以得之者也。彼有爲昏迷不恭者，怠棄三正者，狎侮五常、怠荒弗敬者，何惑乎安其所危而不自知耶？嗚呼！克畏則聖，弗畏則狂；克畏則治，弗畏則亂。其機如此，有天下者曷其奈何弗敬？
translation_en:
…yet he treasures neither objects from distant lands nor exotic things: in guarding against indolence and neglect and taking care to cultivate virtue, he dares allow himself no license. Ever vigilant, what action does he take without apprehension? It is not that he fails to realize that none under Heaven opposes him and that he could therefore act without restraint. In his heart he firmly says: “What Heaven has bestowed upon me is no comfortable position given for my enjoyment. It has truly bequeathed to me the greatest responsibility and cast me into the greatest difficulty. If I indulge even a single thought, every action will go astray. Heaven’s reprimands and warnings will then arrive; at worst, its grant of sovereignty will end. How could I fail to feel fear and apprehension?” How profound it is that a ruler of abundant virtue must have something to hold in awe whenever he acts!

Examining antiquity, we find that Yao’s virtue was already far-reaching, yet he reverently followed Heaven and respectfully gave the people the seasons: this was how he remained ever cautious. Shun’s virtue was already without fault, yet he consulted the Four Peaks and the regional governors: this was how he remained ever watchful. Yu’s civilizing instruction had already spread abroad, yet he revered virtue and diligently faced difficulties: this was how he remained tireless. Tang’s virtue already shone brilliantly, yet he neither drew near to sensual pleasures nor accumulated wealth: this was how he remained apprehensive. All the people lived in harmony, and all within the Four Seas enjoyed enduring peace; government had already attained perfection. Yet Kings Wen and Wu had no leisure even to eat, and reverence and righteousness prevailed within them: this was how they remained circumspect and maintained their strength. Which of these was not the utmost expression of abundant virtue?

Thus, what enabled emperors and kings to make their great names shine for all eternity was assuredly reverence alone. As for those who were benighted and disrespectful, who negligently abandoned the three proper duties, or who treated the Five Constant Virtues with contempt and were idle, dissolute, and irreverent—why be puzzled that they felt secure in their peril without knowing it? Alas! The capacity for awe makes a sage; its absence makes a madman. The capacity for awe brings order; its absence brings disorder. Such is the hinge upon which these outcomes turn. How, then, can anyone who possesses all under Heaven fail to be reverent?

translation_en:
Memorial
A model memorial of thanks on behalf of the Song chief councillors upon receiving the imperially composed Essentials for the Crown Prince (Chenghua yaolüe). 〔Third year of Tianxi, 1019〕
By Wang Yanchong.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: In expressing thanks, the author sets forth the essential principles of educating the heir apparent. His literary imagination is luxuriant, his language serene, and his rhythms and parallel phrases resonant. This is among the most accomplished examples of four–six parallel prose. Let it be included; it could well be transmitted alongside Song memorials.

Comment by Associate Examiner Hou, Instructor: Examination compositions in the memorial genre frequently recycle stock formulas and are exceedingly tiresome to read. This piece follows proper models in recounting antiquity and grounds its praise in evidence. Its parallel phrases are sonorous, and its meaning is fully and clearly expressed. No admonitions or models could be more pertinent to assisting the heir apparent. It should be included.

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: The exposition is precise and pertinent, the form elevated and antique, the diction rich and splendid, and the rhythms resonant. This is among the finest examples of four–six parallel prose and certainly deserves selection at a high rank.

We humbly reflect that the Crown Prince nurtures his virtue, grandly inheriting a plan for ten thousand generations; Your Majesty’s splendid composition unfolds its brilliance, clearly displaying the standards of a sovereign. Your provision for posterity bestows blessings upon the imperial succession; your magnificent writing showers radiant favor upon your ministers. Its Way accords with the transmission of the heart; its brilliance makes us rub our eyes in wonder. We, your servants So-and-so and the others, in utmost awe and trepidation, bow our heads and knock our foreheads upon the ground.
We respectfully consider that the Book of Changes honors the heir who presides over the sacrificial wine, continuing the foundations of the ancestral temple and the altars of soil and grain; the rites take care over the instruction of the heir apparent, clarifying the Way governing fathers and sons, rulers and ministers. Only the Three Kings were able to instruct their heirs early; hence their realms enjoyed enduring order and peace for a thousand years. Reverently continuing the Way of Yu is clearly attested in the canonical rules; keeping Tang’s example constantly in view likewise supplies instruction against wayward habits and faults. Looking further at the flourishing Way of Zhou, we find the educational institutions of Yu still more fully developed. Instruction in dances with shields and spears, feathers and flutes, and in the Odes and Documents, invariably came at the proper times; the great jade disks and celestial jade spheres, and the displayed charts and admonitions, seem still before our eyes. King Wen’s plans and King Wu’s achievements offered guidance and protection, their presence perceived even in soup and walls. The Duke of Shao as Grand Protector and the Grand Duke as Grand Preceptor solemnly supplied admonitions and rules, extending even to the armrest and staff. In rising and retiring, going out and coming in, nothing lacked reverence. Thus the heir became respectful and courteous, gentle and refined: his accomplishment brought delight [?].
As successive later dynasties passed, few carried on these earlier traditions. In the Han lecture tent, the classics were expounded, magnificently observing the rites that esteemed tutors and honored teachers. Even under a dynasty possessing only a remnant of sovereignty, likened to the secondary color purple [?], there was a compilation of the Essential Record of the Crown Prince’s Palace. 熈朝。此蓋伏遇天縱神明，日新敬德，赤文綠字，恭膺河洛之符；玉振金聲，懋建中和之極。聖盡倫，王盡制，誕敷言以錫民；親則父，尊則君，肆受祉而及子。

乃眷元良之重，夙鍾岐嶷之英。視膳三朝，仁孝方隆于睿德；觀書乙夜，聰明允愜于宸衷。念貽謀之克臧，則開卷而有益。爰及政機之暇，載披冊府之藏。運思陶鈞，六籍具陳于掌上；游神竹素，十行親動于毫端。監成憲以無愆，次舊聞而弗闕。謂主器先于謹習，謂務學在于宗經。陳道德仁義之微，示戒懼謙恭之則。若節情養性以修其身
translation_en:
…this glorious dynasty. We have indeed been privileged to encounter Your Majesty, endowed by Heaven with spiritual insight, daily renewing your reverent cultivation of virtue. Through red markings and green script, you reverently receive the auspicious tokens of the Yellow River and the Luo River; with the resonance of jade chimes and bronze bells, you diligently establish the supreme standard of equilibrium and harmony. As sage, you fulfill all human relationships; as king, you perfect all institutions, broadly promulgating your words to benefit the people. In familial affection you are a father; in dignity you are a sovereign. Thus you receive blessings and extend them to your son.

You turn your attention to the weighty position of the heir apparent, in whom exceptional intelligence was manifest from infancy. Attending to your meals and paying his respects three times daily, he increasingly displays benevolence and filial devotion in his sagely virtue; reading books during the second watch of the night, his intelligence truly satisfies your imperial heart. Mindful that plans bequeathed to posterity must be sound, you ensure that opening the book brings benefit. Thus, in intervals free from affairs of government, you have examined the holdings of the imperial library. Applying your thoughts with the shaping power of a potter’s wheel, you hold the Six Classics fully arrayed in your hands; letting your mind range through the written records, you personally set the ten lines of imperial writing flowing from your brush. You scrutinize established precedents to avoid error and arrange inherited accounts so that nothing is omitted. You declare that bearing responsibility for the ancestral vessels requires, above all, careful practice, and that pursuing learning consists in taking the Classics as one’s foundation. You expound the subtleties of the Way, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness, and set forth standards of vigilance, apprehension, humility, and reverence. Such matters as moderating the emotions and nurturing one’s nature in order to cultivate oneself…

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之士非子也耶取之
人君有畏天之心尤貴有應天之政惟應
天以政而後天心之仁愛不孤夫遇災而
懼不敢荒寧凛然上帝之臨汝者畏天之
心也側身厲行上下交修布德而致之民
者應天之政也心以本之政以達之則民
心悅而天意得矣昔之顯然而示者不將
有其變而無其應哉是道也考諸帝王而
不謬質諸
===
祖
宗而無疑此我
皇上之所當祖述而憲章者也請敬陳之嘗觀
書之胤征曰先王克謹天戒易之震曰洊
雷震君子以恐懼修省易書所稱皆慎重
天戒之意也明此於唐則爲堯之儆予夫
帝德廣運嘗得統于天矣又何儆焉而洪
水方割固曰儆予夷攷其時敷治則以命
舜行水則以命禹山澤則以命益稼穡則

之士，非子也耶？取之。

人君有畏天之心，尤貴有應天之政。惟應天以政，而後天心之仁愛不孤。夫遇災而懼，不敢荒寧，凛然上帝之臨汝者，畏天之心也；側身厲行，上下交修，布德而致之民者，應天之政也。心以本之，政以達之，則民心悅而天意得矣。昔之顯然而示者，不將有其變而無其應哉？是道也，考諸帝王而不謬，質諸祖宗而無疑，此我皇上之所當祖述而憲章者也。請敬陳之。嘗觀《書》之《胤征》曰：「先王克謹天戒。」《易》之《震》曰：「洊雷，震；君子以恐懼修省。」《易》《書》所稱，皆慎重天戒之意也。明此於唐，則爲堯之儆予。夫帝德廣運，嘗得統于天矣，又何儆焉？而洪水方割，固曰儆予。夷攷其時，敷治則以命舜，行水則以命禹，山澤則以命益，稼穡則
translation_en:
…a man who speaks frankly and remonstrates to the utmost—is that not you? Accept this essay.

For a ruler to have a heart that stands in awe of Heaven is important; still more precious is government that responds to Heaven. Only by responding to Heaven through government can Heaven’s benevolent care be duly reciprocated. To fear when calamity strikes, to dare not lapse into idle ease, and to stand in trembling awe as though the Lord on High were looking down upon you—this is a heart that fears Heaven. To conduct oneself humbly and earnestly, for those above and below to cultivate themselves together, and to spread beneficence and bring it to the people—this is government that responds to Heaven. With the heart as its foundation and government as its means of expression, the people’s hearts will be gladdened and Heaven’s intent fulfilled. Will not those earlier, conspicuously manifested signs then remain anomalies without the consequences they portended? This way proves sound when tested against the ancient emperors and kings, and admits no doubt when examined against our imperial ancestors. It is what our Emperor should carry forward and take as his model. Allow me respectfully to explain.

I have read in the “Punitive Expedition of Yin” chapter of the Book of Documents: “The former kings were able to heed Heaven’s warnings.” In the “Thunder” hexagram of the Book of Changes it says: “Repeated thunder: Thunder. The gentleman, in fear and trembling, cultivates and examines himself.” What the Changes and the Documents say expresses the same intention: to treat Heaven’s warnings with the utmost care. In the age of Tang, this understanding appeared in Yao’s words, “Warn me.” His imperial virtue was vast and far-reaching, and he had already attained unity with Heaven; what further warning did he need? Yet when the floodwaters were wreaking destruction, he indeed said, “Warn me.” Examining that time, we find that he charged Shun with extending good government, Yu with channeling the waters, Yi with the mountains and marshes, and, for sowing and harvesting…

text:
以命稷司徒則以命契所以交修者未嘗
不孜孜也明此於商則爲湯之責己夫懋
昭大德天錫勇智矣又奚責焉而大旱致
禱固以自責夷攷其時則引咎于政之不
節民之失職宫室女謁之崇盛苞苴讒夫
之肆行且置一德之相鑄莊山之金所以
修政者又未嘗不急急也是二聖人者何
嘗不修德以回天哉洪惟我
太祖高皇帝開天立極受
===
命之初日昃不遑觀其因七政之紊度也則
下求言之
詔以聞過遇水旱之相仍也則有侍臣省臣之
諭以責躬而又
命儒臣爲存心省躬二錄焉存心錄者則紀
歷代帝王祭祀之感召祥異者也欲後世
之爲君者知災異爲天心之譴告思所以
致感之由求所以消復之道耳省躬錄者
則紀歷代災異之應于臣下者也欲後世

…he entrusted Ji with this charge, and appointed Xie as Minister of Instruction. In their joint efforts to put matters right, they were never less than diligent. In the Shang, this understanding found expression in Tang’s reproaching himself. He had illustriously displayed great virtue, and Heaven had bestowed courage and wisdom upon him: what further cause had he for self-reproach? Yet when a great drought prompted him to pray, he indeed reproached himself. Examining that time, we find that he took the blame for government’s lack of restraint, the people’s loss of their livelihoods, the extravagance of palaces and the influence of women’s intercessions, and the unchecked prevalence of bribes and slanderers. Moreover, he appointed a minister of undivided virtue and cast currency from the metal of Mount Zhuang. In his efforts to reform government, he was never less than urgent. Did these two sages ever fail to cultivate virtue in order to turn Heaven’s will?
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao inaugurated a new order and established the supreme standard. From the beginning of his receipt of Heaven’s mandate, he had no leisure even when the sun declined. When the seven celestial luminaries strayed from their proper courses, he issued an edict soliciting counsel so that he might hear of his faults. When floods and droughts followed one another, he issued instructions to attendant and provincial officials [?], reproaching himself. He further ordered his scholarly officials to compile two records: Preserving the Mind and Examining Oneself. 秦人否耶監司以檢吏治也果能獨持風
裁使饕餮之不爲民蠹否耶守令以寄民
命也果能政平訟理如昔人之獨用寬和
治去太甚洗冤澤物立決疑獄否耶執事
謂大小臣工未能敷宣
德意致然不誠然哉迺猶致疑于
punctuated: 念，遠有以質諸堯舜，□□有以契諸皇祖世宗矣。是宜災變之銷息也。近者淮徐之水，浩浩懷襄；荆揚之旱，赤地千里。災異日形于奏牘，厥咎何繇哉？吾意聖德已至，而奉承德意者或未之良；聖化已煕，而敷宣化理者猶未之舉也。何也？其在三公，固曰論道經邦矣，果能同心輔政，燮調愆伏否耶？其在六卿，固曰分職率屬矣，果能克倡羣牧，阜成兆民否耶？撫臣以通下情也，果能體恤民隱，不爲越人之視秦人否耶？監司以核吏治也，果能獨持風裁，使饕餮之不爲民蠹否耶？守令以寄民命也，果能政平訟理，如昔人之獨用寛和，治去太甚，洗冤澤物，立决疑獄否耶？執事謂大小臣工未能敷宣德意致然，不誠然哉？廼猶致疑于
translation_en:
…this resolve reaches back to bear scrutiny against Yao and Shun, and □□ accords with the imperial ancestor, Emperor Shizong. Thus disasters and anomalies ought to subside. Recently, however, the floodwaters of Huai and Xu have surged far and wide, engulfing the land, while drought in Jing and Yang has left the earth parched for a thousand li. Disasters and anomalies appear daily in memorials to the throne. Where does the fault lie? I believe that the sage sovereign’s virtue has reached perfection, but those charged with carrying out his virtuous intentions may not have done so well; his transforming influence already shines brightly, but those charged with spreading that influence and good government have yet to put them into effect. Why is this?

The Three Dukes are indeed said to deliberate on the Way and order the realm; but can they truly assist in government with one mind and harmonize the irregular workings of the seasons? The Six Ministers are indeed said to divide their responsibilities and lead their subordinates; but can they truly guide the assembled regional administrators and bring prosperity and fulfillment to the myriad people? Grand coordinators are charged with conveying the circumstances of those below; but can they truly show concern for the people’s hidden sufferings, rather than regard them as a person of Yue regards a person of Qin? Surveillance commissioners are charged with examining the administration of officials; but can they truly uphold independent and resolute standards, so that rapacious officials do not prey upon the people? Prefects and magistrates are entrusted with the people’s lives; but can they truly govern equitably and adjudicate lawsuits properly, as men of former times did—relying solely on leniency and harmony, eliminating excessive severity from government, redressing injustices and extending benefits to others, and promptly deciding doubtful cases?

You say that this situation has arisen because officials, great and small, have failed to disseminate and carry out the sovereign’s virtuous intentions. Is that not indeed so? Yet you still cast doubt upon …

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
聖政者此憂治世而危明主牖納約而廣陳言
有以知執事為責難之恭忠愛無已之心
也敢為首鼠之默而不以正對乎愚生則
以今日堯湯之患所猶未免者亦應天之
政疑有所未盡焉仰惟
皇上敬畏崇矣而拒逆忠直尚有如伊訓之所
陳者則從諫弗咈猶未之逮也
儉德慎矣而形諸
詔旨尚有如魯史之求金者則不殖貨利猶
===
===
未之及也民隱恤矣而列諸章奏尚有如
鄭俠之所繪者則遣使賑貸猶未之舉也
刑罰清矣而諸州大辟尚有飛六月之霜
者則錄案聞奏猶未之盡也不然何天心
之仁愛竟如是哉雖然有儆予之堯矣亦
必有儉勤之禹而後可以底天下於平成
有責己之湯矣亦必有一德之尹而後可
以致兆民於允殖百官修輔夏后之山川
所以寧也庶正鞠哉宣王之旱魃所以息

punctuated: 聖政者，此憂治世而危明主，牖納約而廣陳言，有以知執事為責難之恭、忠愛無已之心也。敢為首鼠之默，而不以正對乎？愚生則以今日堯湯之患所猶未免者，亦應天之政疑有所未盡焉。仰惟皇上敬畏崇矣，而拒逆忠直，尚有如伊訓之所陳者，則從諫弗咈，猶未之逮也；儉德慎矣，而形諸詔旨，尚有如魯史之求金者，則不殖貨利，猶未之及也；民隱恤矣，而列諸章奏，尚有如鄭俠之所繪者，則遣使賑貸，猶未之舉也；刑罰清矣，而諸州大辟，尚有飛六月之霜者，則錄案聞奏，猶未之盡也。不然，何天心之仁愛竟如是哉？雖然，有儆予之堯矣，亦必有儉勤之禹，而後可以底天下於平成；有責己之湯矣，亦必有一德之尹，而後可以致兆民於允殖。百官修輔，夏后之山川所以寧也；庶正鞠哉，宣王之旱魃所以息
translation_en:
…the sage sovereign’s governance: this is to feel concern even for an orderly age and apprehension even for an enlightened ruler, finding an opening through which to offer restrained counsel while setting forth your views extensively. From this I recognize in you the respect shown by demanding difficult accomplishments of the sovereign, and a heart whose loyalty and affection know no end. Dare I remain silent in vacillation rather than give an upright reply? This humble student believes that, if we have still not escaped calamities like those of Yao and Tang today, there may also be something not yet fully accomplished in the policies by which we respond to Heaven.

Reverently considering His Majesty: his reverence and awe are exalted; yet if there are still instances of rejecting and opposing the loyal and upright, like those described in the Instructions of Yi (Yi xun), then he has not yet attained the ideal of following remonstrance without resisting it. He carefully cultivates frugality; yet if his edicts still contain demands like the request for gold recorded in the annals of Lu, then he has not yet attained the ideal of refraining from accumulating wealth and profit. He shows compassion for the people’s hidden sufferings; yet if memorials still report conditions like those depicted by Zheng Xia, then the dispatch of envoys to distribute relief and loans has still not been carried out. His punishments are administered with clarity; yet if capital sentences in the various prefectures still cause frost to fall in the sixth month, then the review of cases and reporting of them to the throne have still not been fully accomplished. Otherwise, why would Heaven’s benevolent concern manifest itself in precisely this way?

Nevertheless, even with a Yao who says, “Admonish me,” there must also be a Yu, frugal and diligent, before the realm can be brought to peace and order. Even with a Tang who reproaches himself, there must also be a Yi Yin of undivided virtue before the myriad people can truly be made to flourish. The hundred officials diligently fulfilled their duties and assisted their ruler: this was why the mountains and rivers under the sovereign of Xia were brought to tranquility. The various chief officials exerted themselves: this was why the drought demon of King Xuan was made to cease…

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
也今之從政者可得泄泄然莫之省憂哉
愚生覆幬于堯天之下而鼓舞于鈞天之
盛不自知其狂也故肆言至此唯執事不
錄其罪矜其愚而進教之焉
第二問
朱一儒
同考試官進士霍批文事武備歸本責實
乃當今切要之論子能陳之誠識時務之俊傑也錄之
考試官修撰申批視學閱兵一代盛典我
===

祖烈而舉行之子能援古證今根究本實具見卓識取之不獨以其文也
考試官右諭德丁批文武並用長久之術也我
皇上臨幸太學
大閱營兵可謂祖述帝王憲章
二祖矣子能恭紀其盛末尤惓惓於揆文奮武之實此知本之士也允宜錄之
盖聞帝王之敷治也有崇文之盛節有經

甚設矣而非為容也治兵習旅討國人而

… Can those who serve in government today remain complacent, giving this neither reflection nor concern? I, an ignorant student, dwell beneath the shelter of a heaven like Yao’s and rejoice in the splendor of celestial music. Unaware of my own presumption, I have therefore spoken freely to this extent. I ask only that you, honored examiners, overlook my offense, take pity on my ignorance, and grant me further instruction.
Second Policy Question
Zhu Yiru
Comment by Associate Examiner Huo, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi): “To trace civil affairs and military preparedness to their foundations and demand substantive results is an argument of pressing importance today. We select you for more than your literary accomplishment alone.”

Our emperor has visited the Imperial University in person and held a grand review of the garrison troops. title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
訓之其法甚備矣而非為夸也本之實心
而施之為實政故能作人勵世建威銷萌
陳一代之上儀垂萬世之良法文教蔚隆
武功丕赫良有繇巳夫不惟其實而迹是
循則視學為彌文而閱兵為壯觀豈所語
帝王之道哉且視學閱兵之制所從来遠
矣大戴禮保傅篇曰帝入東學尚親而貴
仁帝入西學尚賢而貴德帝入南學尚齒
而貴信帝入北學尚貴而尊爵帝入太學
===
承師而問道言先王視學若斯之勤也而
其說尤詳于禮經以釋奠則視學禮不曰
祭先師先聖乎以養老則視學禮不曰養
老于東序乎以習樂舞則視學禮不曰入
學合舞頒學合聲乎以簡不率教則視學
禮不曰移之郊遂屏之遠方乎盖先王非
具儀爾也以立教也是故尊聖道以正人
心致孝弟以興民行宣布中和以陶鎔其
氣質明示彰瘅以黙奪其非邪俾天下承

心致孝弟以興民行宣布中和以陶鎔其
氣質明示彰癉以黙奪其非邪俾天下承
punctuated:
訓之，其法甚備矣，而非為夸也。本之實心，而施之為實政，故能作人勵世，建威銷萌，陳一代之上儀，垂萬世之良法。文教蔚隆，武功丕赫，良有繇巳。夫不惟其實而迹是循，則視學為彌文，而閱兵為壯觀，豈所語帝王之道哉？且視學閱兵之制，所從来遠矣。
大戴禮保傅篇曰：「帝入東學，尚親而貴仁；帝入西學，尚賢而貴德；帝入南學，尚齒而貴信；帝入北學，尚貴而尊爵；帝入太學，承師而問道。」言先王視學若斯之勤也。而其說尤詳于禮經。以釋奠，則視學禮不曰「祭先師先聖」乎？以養老，則視學禮不曰「養老于東序」乎？以習樂舞，則視學禮不曰「入學合舞，頒學合聲」乎？以簡不率教，則視學禮不曰「移之郊遂，屏之遠方」乎？盖先王非具儀爾也，以立教也。是故尊聖道以正人心，致孝弟以興民行，宣布中和以陶鎔其氣質，明示彰瘅以黙奪其非邪，俾天下承
translation_en:
…and instruct them: their regulations were thoroughly comprehensive, yet were not intended for ostentation. Grounded in sincere intentions and implemented as substantive government, these measures could nurture worthy men and inspire the age, establish authority and extinguish incipient disorder, display the supreme ceremonies of a dynasty, and bequeath sound standards for all generations. The flourishing of civil instruction and the brilliance of military achievements indeed had their source in this. If one attends only to outward precedents without considering their substance, however, an imperial visit to the schools becomes mere ceremonial elaboration, and a review of troops becomes a grand spectacle. Could this be what is meant by the Way of emperors and kings? Moreover, the institutions of visiting the schools and reviewing troops have origins in the distant past.
The “Protector and Tutor” chapter of the Elder Dai’s Record of Rites states: “When the emperor enters the eastern school, he esteems kinship and values benevolence; when he enters the western school, he esteems worthiness and values virtue; when he enters the southern school, he esteems seniority and values trustworthiness; when he enters the northern school, he esteems noble standing and honors rank; when he enters the Great School, he attends upon his teacher and inquires about the Way.” This describes how diligently the former kings visited the schools. The explanation is especially detailed in the ritual classics. Regarding the offering ceremony for former sages and teachers, do not the rites for visiting the schools say, “Sacrifice to the former teachers and former sages”? Regarding care for the elderly, do they not say, “Care for the elderly in the eastern school”? Regarding practice in music and dance, do they not say, “Enter the school and coordinate the dances; at the school [?], coordinate the voices”? Regarding the identification of those who fail to follow instruction, do they not say, “Remove them to the outlying districts and banish them to distant regions”? The former kings were not merely furnishing ceremonial forms; they were establishing moral instruction. Thus they honored the Way of the sages to rectify people’s hearts, promoted filial piety and fraternal respect to elevate popular conduct, disseminated equilibrium and harmony to mold people’s temperaments, and clearly displayed the commendation of good and condemnation of evil to quietly dispel their wrongdoing and depravity, so that all under Heaven might receive…

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
流聽風脩弦誦之業章志貞軌游道德之
塗故先王一視學而眾知文教之隆也周
官大司馬法曰中春教振旅遂以蒐田中
夏教茇舍遂以苗田中秋教治兵遂以獮
田中冬教大閱遂以狩田言先王閱兵若
斯之嚴也而其說雜見于諸家王制言天
子歲三田不曰習民于無事乎月令言秋
習五戎冬射御角力不曰講武于農隙乎
臧孫言三年治兵不曰數軍實習威儀乎
===
何休言五年大蒐不曰存不忘亡安不忘
危乎盖先王非徒法爾也以修備也是故
因田致民以示之期會因獵教戰以習其
技能明尊卑先後之列以齊其心定遠近
踈數之節以休其力俾有勇知方篤死綏
之義安制矜節揚敵愾之威故先王一閱
兵而眾知武功之振也由是觀之先王視
學之勤是隆文教之實也其閱兵之嚴是
振武功之實也經傳之所載不同而義一

技能明尊卑先後之列以齊其心定遠近
疏數之節以休其力俾有勇知方篤死綏
之義安制矜節揚敵愾之威故先王一閱
兵而衆知武功之振也由是觀之先王視
學之勤是隆文教之實也其閱兵之嚴是
振武功之實也經傳之所載不同而義一
punctuated:
流聽風，脩弦誦之業，章志貞軌，游道德之塗。故先王一視學，而眾知文教之隆也。
《周官》大司馬法曰：「中春教振旅，遂以蒐田；中夏教茇舍，遂以苗田；中秋教治兵，遂以獮田；中冬教大閱，遂以狩田。」言先王閱兵若斯之嚴也。而其說雜見于諸家。《王制》言天子歲三田，不曰「習民于無事」乎？《月令》言秋習五戎，冬射御角力，不曰「講武于農隙」乎？臧孫言三年治兵，不曰「數軍實，習威儀」乎？何休言五年大蒐，不曰「存不忘亡，安不忘危」乎？盖先王非徒法爾也，以修備也。是故因田致民，以示之期會；因獵教戰，以習其技能；明尊卑先後之列，以齊其心；定遠近踈數之節，以休其力。俾有勇知方，篤死綏之義，安制矜節，揚敵愾之威。故先王一閱兵，而眾知武功之振也。
由是觀之，先王視學之勤，是隆文教之實也；其閱兵之嚴，是振武功之實也。經傳之所載不同，而義一
translation_en:
…receive their influence and heed their example, cultivate the practice of musical accompaniment and recitation, manifest their aspirations and hold to correct patterns of conduct, and travel the path of the Way and virtue. Thus, whenever the former kings inspected the schools, all recognized the flourishing of civil education.
The regulations of the Grand Minister of War in the Offices of Zhou state: “In mid-spring, teach the maneuvers for recalling the troops, and then conduct the spring hunt; in mid-summer, teach encampment, and then conduct the summer hunt; in mid-autumn, teach the ordering of troops, and then conduct the autumn hunt; in mid-winter, teach the grand review, and then conduct the winter hunt.” This describes how rigorous the former kings were in reviewing their troops. Explanations of this are also scattered among various writings. When the “Royal Regulations” says that the Son of Heaven hunts three times a year, does it not speak of “training the people when there is no emergency”? When the “Monthly Ordinances” speaks of practicing with the five kinds of weapons in autumn, and archery, charioteering, and contests of strength in winter, does it not speak of “practicing military affairs during breaks in agricultural work”? When Zangsun speaks of ordering the troops every three years, does he not speak of “counting military resources and practicing proper military bearing”? When He Xiu speaks of a grand hunt every five years, does he not say, “While surviving, do not forget destruction; while secure, do not forget danger”? The former kings were not merely observing regulations: they were maintaining preparedness. Thus they assembled the people through the hunts to acquaint them with appointed times and musters, and taught warfare through hunting to train their skills. They clarified the ranks of superior and inferior, front and rear, to unite their resolve; and regulated distances and the spacing of formations to conserve their strength. They thereby made the people courageous yet mindful of right conduct, steadfast in the duty to die rather than yield ground, at ease with discipline and respectful of restraint, and able to display their might in confronting the enemy. Thus, whenever the former kings reviewed the troops, all recognized the vigor of their military achievements.
Viewed in this light, the former kings’ diligence in inspecting schools was the substance of their promotion of civil education; their rigor in reviewing troops was the substance of their strengthening of military achievement. What the classics and commentaries record differs, but the meaning is one…

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
也乃周禮不言視□□□上春舍菜合舞鼓
徵學士固視學事□□魯之大閱以諸侯僭
天子之禮則春秋譏焉故舉其實雖沒其
名可也是周禮所不詳也循其名而失其
實不可也是春秋所不予也昔武王勝殷
遏劉耆定厥功矣而干戈載櫜辟雍乃興
其詩曰鎬京辟雍皇王烝哉宣王修文武
之業周道粲然興焉乃東都行狩大簡師
徒其詩曰徒御不驚有聞無聲天下稱武
===
王之烈而頌宣王中興之功者以關雎麟
趾之意行周官法度也漢唐願治之主非
不慕循其遺迹然實不至而有侈心焉明
帝尊養更老袒割辟雍之上禮文煥焉可
述而莫能舉三代之隆其所為教淺也玄
宗躬擐戎服講武驪山戈甲耀天地而莫
能遏漁陽之鋒其所為備疎也彼一時所
施樹非不震耀國都張皇史冊而豈帝王
致治之實哉我

translation_en:
…yet their meaning is one. Now the Rites of Zhou does not speak of inspecting the schools [?]. Its provisions for offering vegetables in the first month of spring, assembling dancers, and summoning students by drum certainly concern inspecting the schools [?]. But when Lu held its grand military review, a feudal lord usurped the rites of the Son of Heaven, and the Spring and Autumn Annals censured it. Thus, to carry out the substance, even without retaining the name, is acceptable: this is what the Rites of Zhou does not describe in detail. To follow the name while losing the substance is unacceptable: this is what the Spring and Autumn Annals refuses to sanction.

In former times, King Wu conquered Yin, checked the slaughter, and firmly established his achievement. Then shields and spears were put away in their cases, and the Biyong royal academy arose. The ode says: “At Haojing’s Biyong, how magnificent was the august king!” King Xuan renewed the work of Kings Wen and Wu, and the Way of Zhou flourished in splendor. Then he went hunting at the eastern capital and held a grand review of his troops. The ode says: “The foot soldiers and charioteers were unperturbed; commands were heard, but there was no clamor.” The reason all under Heaven praised King Wu’s exploits and celebrated King Xuan’s achievement in restoring the dynasty was that they implemented the institutions and rules of the Offices of Zhou in the spirit of the odes “Guanju” (The Calling Ospreys) and “Linzhi” (The Qilin’s Hoofs).

The rulers of Han and Tang who aspired to good government certainly admired these precedents and wished to follow them. Yet they failed to attain their substance and harbored extravagant ambitions. Emperor Ming honored and supported the venerable elders, baring his arm and carving meat for them in the Biyong. The brilliance of his ceremonial observances deserved to be recorded, yet he could not bring about the flourishing conditions of the Three Dynasties, because his instruction was superficial. Xuanzong personally donned military dress and conducted military exercises at Mount Li. Weapons and armor dazzled Heaven and Earth, yet he could not check the armed onslaught from Yuyang, because his preparations were inadequate. What these rulers instituted in their day certainly awed and dazzled their capitals and filled the historical records with grand display. But was it the substance by which true emperors and kings achieved good government? Our …

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
太祖經始皇業也嘗習師江淮耀兵中原威靈
輝達巳乃投戈講藝息馬論道孳孳焉觀
夫大位甫正即隆釋奠之儀太學告成再
舉臨幸之禮非以武功而兼文德者歟我
成祖潤色太平也盖服崇皮弁碑紀視學禮文
咸秩矣乃陳師鞠旅校技程良汲汲焉觀
夫鳴鑾楊林屢閱于邊境癸卯甲辰載閱
于
京師非以文事而兼武備者歟至于敦敘彝
===
倫表章經籍制禮作樂重道親儒則
二祖之崇文教皆實政也攘夷安夏掃穴犁庭
勝算動若神明經畧周乎徼塞則
二祖之修武功皆實政也我
皇上祖述憲章文武並用自紀元之歲即
親幸太學崇祀
先師盛臨觀之文秩坐講之禮于時俎豆升
馨橋門竦聽究皇儀而展帝容隆師道而
訓儒術即有聲之詩不足紀其盛矣已又

馨橋門竦聽究皇儀而展帝容隆師道而
訓儒術即有聲之詩不足紀其盛矣已又
punctuated:
太祖經始皇業也，嘗習師江淮，耀兵中原，威靈輝達。巳乃投戈講藝，息馬論道，孳孳焉。觀夫大位甫正，即隆釋奠之儀；太學告成，再舉臨幸之禮，非以武功而兼文德者歟？我成祖潤色太平也，盖服崇皮弁，碑紀視學，禮文咸秩矣。乃陳師鞠旅，校技程良，汲汲焉。觀夫鳴鑾楊林，屢閱于邊境；癸卯甲辰，載閱于京師，非以文事而兼武備者歟？至于敦敘彝倫，表章經籍，制禮作樂，重道親儒，則二祖之崇文教皆實政也；攘夷安夏，掃穴犁庭，勝算動若神明，經畧周乎徼塞，則二祖之修武功皆實政也。
我皇上祖述憲章，文武並用，自紀元之歲，即親幸太學，崇祀先師，盛臨觀之文，秩坐講之禮。于時俎豆升馨，橋門竦聽，究皇儀而展帝容，隆師道而訓儒術，即《有聲》之詩不足紀其盛矣。已又
translation_en:
…Taizu, in laying the foundations of the imperial enterprise, trained his armies in the Jiang–Huai region and displayed his forces in the Central Plain, his awe-inspiring might shining far and wide. Then he laid aside his weapons to study the arts, rested his horses to discuss the Way, and applied himself diligently. Consider how, as soon as his accession to the throne was secured, he exalted the ceremonial offerings to the ancient sages and teachers; when the Imperial University was completed, he again performed the ceremony of an imperial visit. Was this not the complementing of military achievement with civil virtue?
Our Chengzu, in embellishing an age of peace, honored ceremonial dress by wearing the leather cap [?], and commemorated his visit to the Imperial University in a stele inscription: all ceremonial observances were duly ordered. Then he arrayed his armies and mustered his troops, tested their skills and assessed their excellence, applying himself assiduously. Consider how his carriage bells sounded at Yanglin as he repeatedly reviewed troops along the frontier; in the guimao and jiachen years, he also reviewed them in the capital. Was this not the complementing of civil affairs with military preparedness?
As for strengthening and ordering the enduring human relationships, honoring and elucidating the canonical writings, establishing rites and making music, esteeming the Way and drawing Confucian scholars close: the two ancestral emperors’ promotion of civil instruction consisted entirely of substantive measures of government. Repelling the foreign peoples and securing the Chinese realm, sweeping away enemy lairs and plowing up their courts, devising plans for victory with seemingly divine insight, and extending strategic management throughout the frontier: the two ancestral emperors’ cultivation of military achievement likewise consisted entirely of substantive measures of government.
Our present emperor follows and takes as his model his ancestors’ precedents, employing both civil and military means. From the very first year of his reign, he personally visited the Imperial University, offered exalted sacrifices to the First Teacher, enhanced the ceremonial splendor of his visit, and duly ordered the rite of sitting to hear lectures. At that time, fragrant offerings rose from the sacrificial vessels, and those gathered at the university’s bridge gate listened with reverent attention. He fully manifested imperial dignity and displayed the sovereign’s bearing, exalted the standing of teachers and promoted Confucian learning. Even the ode “There Is Renown” (You sheng) could not adequately record this magnificence. Thereafter, he also…

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
親屈萬乘
大閱三營程將卒之能明賞罰之格于時材
武雲集號令風馳王驅肅而師律嚴天聲
動而士氣作即車攻之雅不足揚其休矣
由是以弘宣教術賁飾鴻猷敷鬯威靈綏
警遠邇則武宣易為而漢唐不足齒也然
執事猶患儒效闊疏戎備衰弛欲聞致治
之實則愚也請畢其說可乎愚聞之戒眾
者先鼓作也赴響者急節應也上作而下
===
應是以教喻于不言而威伸于不戰今家
塾黨庠塗歌里誦髦士固烝烝眾矣列屯
坐食荷戈被甲而趨見為兵者非少矣
主上躬觀辟雍親履行陣而勸率訓厲之意非
不切矣然績效罕睹何也夫亦儀法雖存
而實未至乎且夫肅然而臨儼然而退則
是志意不相孚也已行而遂輟乍舉而旋
廢則是法不可為恒也上所督望在彼而
下猶因恬塞責于此□是本末相鑿也故

punctuated:
親屈萬乘，大閱三營，程將卒之能，明賞罰之格。于時材武雲集，號令風馳，王驅肅而師律嚴，天聲動而士氣作，即《車攻》之雅不足揚其休矣。由是以弘宣教術，賁飾鴻猷，敷鬯威靈，綏警遠邇，則武宣易為，而漢唐不足齒也。然執事猶患儒效闊疏，戎備衰弛，欲聞致治之實，則愚也請畢其說，可乎？愚聞之：戒眾者先鼓作也，赴響者急節應也。上作而下應，是以教喻于不言，而威伸于不戰。
今家塾黨庠，塗歌里誦，髦士固烝烝眾矣；列屯坐食，荷戈被甲而趨見為兵者，非少矣。主上躬觀辟雍，親履行陣，而勸率訓厲之意非不切矣。然績效罕睹，何也？夫亦儀法雖存，而實未至乎？且夫肅然而臨，儼然而退，則是志意不相孚也；已行而遂輟，乍舉而旋廢，則是法不可為恒也；上所督望在彼，而下猶因恬塞責于此，□是本末相鑿也。故
translation_en:
…he personally condescended, in his imperial dignity, to hold a grand review of the Three Training Divisions, assessing the abilities of commanders and soldiers and making clear the standards for rewards and punishments. Martial talent then gathered like clouds, and commands sped like the wind. The royal procession was solemn and military discipline strict; imperial might stirred, and the soldiers’ spirits rose. Even the ode “Chariot Attack” (Che gong) could not adequately celebrate this glory. By these means, he broadly promulgated the arts of instruction, adorned his great designs, extended his awe-inspiring power, and brought reassurance and warning to those far and near. Thus the achievements of Emperors Wu and Xuan would be easy to match, and those of the Han and Tang would scarcely merit mention. Yet you, honored examiners, still worry that Confucian learning produces remote and impractical results and that military preparations have deteriorated. You wish to hear what substance is needed to achieve good government. May I, in my ignorance, set forth the remainder of my argument? I have heard that one who alerts the multitude first sounds the drum, while those who respond to its sound promptly act in time with its beat. When those above initiate and those below respond, instruction is understood without words, and authority extends without battle.
Today there are household schools and community schools, singing along the roads and recitation in the villages; accomplished scholars are indeed abundant. Nor are there few men stationed in garrisons and maintained on provisions, bearing spears and wearing armor, who hasten to present themselves as soldiers. Our sovereign personally visits the Imperial University and walks among the military formations; his intention to encourage, lead, instruct, and spur them on is certainly earnest. Yet why are results so seldom seen? Is it perhaps that, although ceremonies and regulations remain, their substance has not been attained? If he arrives in solemnity and withdraws in stately dignity, then intentions and aspirations fail to inspire mutual trust. If a measure is implemented and then halted, newly instituted and promptly abandoned, then its rules cannot be maintained consistently. If what those above demand and expect lies in one direction, while those below remain complacent and merely discharge their duties perfunctorily in another, [illegible character] this means that root and branch clash with one another. title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
曰實未至也古之帝王獨運陶鈞之上而
衆庶回心端拱深穆之中而方外震懾何
哉以實心行實政耳是故視學之儀不可
廢矣而戶牖箴規羹墻見聖所以重道也
廣厦細旃明師勸誦所以崇儒也虛懷側
席舉孝興廉所以作人也放黜異端宣明
正學所以善世也此揆文之實也大閱之
法所必舉矣而握紀執樞臂運指使所以
决勝也推轂授鉞拊髀良將所以折衝也
===
令如金石信如四時所以定志也風行霆
擊誅賞不測所以厲衆也此奮武之實也
由是以庠序之政責之師儒而詳延方正
博聞之士充其選焉以營伍之政責之將

…it is said: substantive achievement has not yet been attained. The emperors and kings of antiquity alone wielded the potter’s wheel of government from above, and the multitude turned their hearts toward them; they sat solemnly with folded hands in profound stillness, and those beyond their realm trembled in awe. Why? Simply because they carried out substantive policies with sincere hearts. Thus, the ceremonial visit to the schools cannot be abandoned. Yet admonitions at doors and windows, and seeing the sages in one’s soup and upon the wall, are how one honors the Way; spacious halls and fine felt mats, enlightened teachers and encouragement to recite the classics, are how one esteems Confucian learning; an open mind and a seat left vacant in expectation of worthy men, promoting the filial and raising up the incorruptible, are how one nurtures talent; banishing heterodox teachings and making orthodox learning manifest are how one improves the world. These constitute the substance of directing civil culture. The institution of the grand military review must likewise be observed. Yet holding the guiding principles and controlling the central command, so that forces respond as the arm moves the fingers, is how one secures victory; ceremonially pushing a departing general’s carriage and granting him the battle-axe of command, and slapping one’s thigh in longing for a fine general, are how one repels aggression; commands firm as metal and stone, and trustworthiness regular as the four seasons, are how one steadies men’s resolve; moving like the wind and striking like thunder, with punishments and rewards that cannot be anticipated, are how one spurs the troops. These constitute the substance of invigorating military power.

Accordingly, responsibility for administering the schools should be assigned to Confucian teachers, and upright, broadly learned men should be carefully invited to fill those posts. Responsibility for administering military units should be assigned to commanders, and ministers as fierce as bears and unwavering in loyalty should be carefully chosen to undertake those duties. When an enlightened ruler demands substantive achievement above, and the civil and military officials cultivate it below in response, will there be no scholars throughout the realm, wearing their scholarly caps and possessing a foundation in virtue and statecraft, who come forth bearing presentation gifts to enter service? Will there be no armored warriors, endowed with extraordinary ability, intelligence, courage, and strategy, who rise to action, leaping over obstacles? At this point, civil education and military achievements will keep pace with those of Emperors Wu and Xuan and add glory to the two ancestral emperors. Can visits to the schools and reviews of the troops be merely matters of ceremony and prescribed forms? Thus it is said: “The sage king does not allow reputation to exceed actual results.” This is what that means. Respectfully submitted in reply.

Wang Lianggu 王良估

title: 隆慶四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
祖訓畫一而守之久矣今更制易法則有紛亂
約束之譏以義斷恩則有削疎骨肉之罪
忍而坐視則蠹耗愈甚卒有土崩之憂僅
而補緝則苟幸旦夕不救衝決之禍故雖
計臣謀士莫爲破盈庭之言而建必然之
畫者難之也雖然釋今弗圖則後世之難
且十百此矣請試言之漢初諸侯王置吏
握兵同制天子其患在强大而不掉自武
帝推恩分王則宗室子弟莫不受地矣然
===
王之庶子間爲列侯侯之庶子絕無爵土
有去而爲民者有爲民而復仕于朝者自
是而後無諸侯王之患亦無養宗室之費
其經制定也唐之末也帝裔王支流播民
間其患在離渙而不屬自宋養之京師則
五葉之後騷然煩費矣其後辨親疎之等
明襲序之法袒免以下不復賜名敦宗之
院散居郡□□以宋雖費于前而大省于後
其救弊果□□是言之勢有所必極極則
